before.title: Polynomial singular decay with power and logarithmic source balls
before.statement:
For this example put $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. On real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, let $e_j$ be the coordinate vectors and define $K_ax=(j^{-a}x_j)_{j\ge1}$ for $a>0$. For $
u,q,ho>0$, the power source ball $X_{
u,ho}(K_a):=\{|K_a|^
u w:\|w\|_2\leho\}$ has coordinates $x_j=j^{-a
u}w_j$, while the logarithmic source ball $X_{\log,q,ho}(K_a):=\{\psi_q(|K_a|)w:\|w\|_2\leho\}$, where $\psi_q(0)=0$ and $\psi_q(t)=(1+\log(1/t))^{-q}$ for $0<t\le1$, has coordinates $x_j=(1+a\log j)^{-q}w_j$. The operator is compact and injective with $\|K_a\|=1$. For the power ball the centered modulus has the bound in the conditional-modulus theorem, with equality at $\delta_j=ho j^{-a(
u+1)}$; this does not assert equality for every $\delta$.

before.title: Exact worst-case risk of the truncated estimator
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $\epsilon\ge0$. In the Gaussian sequence inverse model with positive singular numbers $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$, let $Q\ge0$ and let $(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be positive and nondecreasing. For each $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, define the squared sequence risk of the cutoff estimator at $D\in\mathbb N_0$ by
$$R_\theta(D):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2\right].$$
Then its exact worst-case squared sequence risk is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)}R_\theta(D)=\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2},$$
where the sum is $0$ for $D=0$. The supremum is attained by the one-coordinate truth $\theta^\star=(Q/a_{D+1})e_{D+1}$, with $\theta^\star=0$ when $Q=0$.
before.strategy: Split the squared sequence loss into retained-coordinate variance and tail bias, bound the tail by the first omitted weight, and attain that bound on the first omitted coordinate.

references.title: Litao Ding and Peter Mathé, Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions, Lemma 1 and its complete proof, PDF pp. 2–3
Iain M. Johnstone, Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models, §3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12), printed pp. 60–61

before.axiom_use: Countable Choice is inherited through the compact SVD and complete-basis coefficient identification used in the model; the finite-coordinate risk calculation itself is choice-free.

before.title: Power source balls are weighted statistical ellipsoids
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $K:X	o Y$ be a compact operator of infinite rank between real Hilbert spaces, with positive singular values $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\downarrow0$. For every $
u,ho>0$, the coefficient sequences of the minimum-norm power source ball
$$X_{
u,ho}(K)=\{|K|^
u w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\leho\}$$
are exactly
$$\left\{	heta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^{-2
u}	heta_j^2\leho^2ight\}.$$
Thus its ellipsoid weights are $a_j=s_j^{-
u}$, a positive nondecreasing sequence.
before.strategy: Expand the spectral power in the fixed right singular basis for one inclusion, then construct a source vector from the weighted-square-summable coefficients for the reverse inclusion.

before.title: Cutoff risk and minimax RMS error over statistical ellipsoids
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $\epsilon>0$, $Q\ge0$, a nonincreasing sequence $s_j>0$ with $s_j\to0$, and a nondecreasing sequence $a_j>0$. Observe $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ for $j\ge1$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal variables, and let the unknown parameter range over
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
Let $R_*(\epsilon)$ be the square root of the minimax expected squared $\ell^2$ error over all measurable deterministic or randomized estimators from the product Borel data space to $\ell^2$, and put
$$R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)=\left[\inf_{D\in\mathbb N_0}\left\{\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2}\right\}\right]^{1/2},\qquad\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.$$
Then $R_*(\epsilon)\le R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)\le2.2R_*(\epsilon)$.
before.strategy: The exact cutoff-risk formula gives the upper bound. For the lower bound, maximize the coordinatewise box-risk functional under the ellipsoid budget, choose its saturated coordinates as a prefix, bound a cutoff risk by twice this maximum, and use a finite product of endpoint priors with the one-coordinate lemma.

references.title: Litao Ding and Peter Mathé, Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions, §1, equations (3)–(9), and the complete proof in §2, PDF pp. 1–5
Iain M. Johnstone, Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models, 2011 draft, §§4.3–4.6, printed pp. 104–113

before.axiom_use: Countable Choice is inherited through the inverse sequence model and the exact-risk supplier. The finite endpoint prior and the lower-bound calculation use no additional choice.

before.title: Sparse Gaussian scalar certificate and extremal profile

references.title: Yuri I. Ingster and Irina A. Suslina, Minimax nonparametric hypothesis testing for ellipsoids and Besov bodies, ESAIM Probability and Statistics 4 (2000), pp. 87–100

before.statement:
Let $0<q<2$, $\alpha,\beta>0$, $s=\alpha+\beta$, $L=qs-2\beta>0$, and $\kappa=L/(2-q)$. For $z>0$ define
$$a(z)=\frac{z^2\sinh(z^2)-q(\cosh(z^2)-1)}{(2-q)z^2},\qquad b(z)=\frac{z^2\sinh(z^2)-2(\cosh(z^2)-1)}{(2-q)z^q},\qquad \phi(z)=\frac{b(z)}{a(z)}.$$
Both $a$ and $b$ are positive, and for every $v\in\mathbb R$,
$$\cosh(zv)-1\ge a(z)v^2-b(z)|v|^q,$$
with equality at $v=0,z,-z$. The function $\phi:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is continuous and strictly increasing onto its target. Put
$$z(x)=\phi^{-1}(x^L),\qquad \psi(z)=\frac1{2a(z)},\qquad d(x)=x^{2\beta}\psi(z(x))\quad(x>0).$$
For $C=[6(2-q)]^{1/(6-q)}$, its endpoint asymptotics are
$$z(x)\sim Cx^{L/(6-q)},\quad \psi(z)\sim z^{-2}\ (z\downarrow0),\quad d(x)\sim C^{-2}x^{2\beta-2L/(6-q)}\quad(x\downarrow0),$$
$$z(x)\sim x^\kappa,\quad \psi(z)\sim(2-q)e^{-z^2}\ (z\to\infty),\quad d(x)\sim(2-q)x^{2\beta}e^{-z(x)^2}\quad(x\to\infty).$$
There is a constant $C_1$ depending only on the parameters such that
$$\psi(z)z^2\le C_1,\quad \psi(z)(e^{z^2}-1)\le C_1\quad(z>0),\qquad \psi(z)^2(e^{z^2}-1)\le C_1e^{-z^2}\quad(z\ge1).$$
The following improper integrals are finite and positive:
$$c_0=\int_0^\infty d(x)^2(\cosh(z(x)^2)-1)\,dx,\quad c_1=\int_0^\infty d(x)z(x)^2x^{2\beta}\,dx,\quad c_2=\int_0^\infty d(x)z(x)^qx^{qs}\,dx,$$
$$M_1=\int_0^\infty x^{4\beta}d(x)z(x)^4\,dx,\qquad M_2=\int_0^\infty x^{2qs}d(x)z(x)^{2q}\,dx,$$
and $c_0=(c_1-c_2)/2$.

For positive real $n,h_0$, set $z_i=z(i/n)$ and $h_i=h_0d(i/n)$. Then $\sum_i h_i<\infty$, and for every finite real vector $(v_i)_{i\le m}$,
$$\sum_{i\le m}h_i(\cosh(z_iv_i)-1)\ge\frac{h_0}2\left(n^{-2\beta}\sum_{i\le m}i^{2\beta}v_i^2-n^{-qs}\sum_{i\le m}i^{qs}|v_i|^q\right).$$
As $n\to\infty$, the Riemann sums of the five displayed integral integrands, divided by $n$, converge to their respective integrals. In particular,
$$\sum_i h_i^2(\cosh(z_i^2)-1)\sim c_0h_0^2n,\quad \sum_i i^{2\beta}h_iz_i^2\sim c_1h_0n^{2\beta+1},\quad \sum_i i^{qs}h_iz_i^q\sim c_2h_0n^{qs+1},$$
$$\sum_i i^{4\beta}h_iz_i^4\sim M_1h_0n^{4\beta+1},\qquad \sum_i i^{2qs}h_iz_i^{2q}\sim M_2h_0n^{2qs+1}.$$

Let $\varepsilon>0$, $r>0$, and define the relaxed extremal value
$$J_\varepsilon(r)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i\ge1}g_i^2(\cosh(w_i^2)-1):\ 0\le g_i\le1,\ w_i\ge0,\ \sum_i i^{2\beta}g_iw_i^2\ge r^2\varepsilon^{-2},\ \sum_i i^{qs}g_iw_i^q\le\varepsilon^{-q}\right\}.$$
Choose $n,h_0>0$ by
$$c_1h_0n^{2\beta+1}=r^2\varepsilon^{-2},\qquad c_2h_0n^{qs+1}=\varepsilon^{-q},\qquad U^2=c_0h_0^2n.$$
Whenever $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $r\to0$, $n\to\infty$, and $h_0\to0$, one has $J_\varepsilon(r)\sim U^2$. Writing
$$A=2\alpha+1/q-1/2,\qquad B=2s+1/q,\qquad D=\alpha+\beta(1-2/q)=L/q,$$
this gives
$$\sqrt{J_\varepsilon(r)}\sim c\varepsilon^{-A/D}r^{B/D},\qquad c=\frac{\sqrt{c_0}}{c_1}\left(\frac{c_1}{c_2}\right)^{-(2\beta+1/2)/L}>0.$$
The sufficient condition $n\to\infty$, $h_0\to0$ is equivalent to
$$r=o(\varepsilon^{a_c}),\qquad a_c=\frac{q\alpha+1-q/2}{q(\alpha+\beta)+1}.$$
The free coefficients $h_i$ need not be at most one. The upper bound on $J_\varepsilon$ is realized asymptotically by finitely supported feasible pairs, constructed by truncating the profile to compact coordinate windows and adjusting $n,h_0$. No probability statement or unrestricted all-radius power asymptotic is asserted.
before.axiom_use: No choice principle is used. The inverse is unique, and the upper bound uses fixed finite coordinate windows before taking numerical limits.

before.title: Minimax detection risk and separation rate
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and use the Gaussian sequence inverse model with singular values $s_j>0$, inverse-noise weights $\sigma_j=s_j^{-1}$, and parameter coordinates $\theta=(\theta_j)\in\ell^2$. Let $a=(a_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $a_j\to\infty$, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $\sigma_j\to\infty$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta_j=\theta_j/\sigma_j$ and observe $Y_j=Z_j/\sigma_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$, where $Z$ is the normalized observation in the Gaussian sequence inverse model and the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal random variables. For $0<q\le2$ and $r>0$, define
$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$
Test $H_0:\eta=0$ against $H_1:\eta\in\Theta_q(r)$ by a product-Borel measurable randomized test $\psi:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\to[0,1]$, where $\psi(y)$ is the rejection probability. Its type-I error and maximal type-II error are
$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$
A positive family $r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ is a minimax separation rate if $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, while $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to0$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to0$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$.

references.title: Yuri I. Ingster, Theofanis Sapatinas and Irina A. Suslina, Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems, §2, PDF pp. 4–6
Evarist Giné and Richard Nickl, Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models, §6.2.1 and §6.2.3

$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$
Test $H_0:\eta=0$ against $H_1:\eta\in\Theta_q(r)$ by a product-Borel measurable randomized test $\psi:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}\to[0,1]$, where $\psi(y)$ is the rejection probability. Its type-I error and maximal type-II error are
$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$
A positive family $r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ is a minimax separation rate if $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, while $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to0$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to0$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$.

before.title: SOLIT in the mean-zero 2D satellite-gradiometry model
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice.

For a relative satellite radius $R>1$, identify the mean-zero real Fourier coefficients of a function on the unit circle with $X=\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, where the two coordinates at frequency $n$ are its normalized cosine and sine coefficients, and give this space the canonical inner product $\langle(a_n,b_n),(c_n,d_n)\rangle=\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. Interleaving the coordinates identifies it isometrically with real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so $X$ is a real Hilbert space. In these coordinates define the 2D satellite-gradiometry operator by
$$
(T_R(a_n,b_n))_{n\ge1}=(t_n a_n,t_n b_n)_{n\ge1},\qquad t_n=n(n+1)R^{-n-2}.
$$
This is the Fourier-coordinate map for recovering the mean-zero gravitational potential from the radial second derivative measured at relative satellite radius $R$. Take the truth to be the Fourier coefficient sequence of $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$. Its constant coefficient is zero, so the omitted zero-frequency component is not part of this mean-zero model. The per-frequency eigenvalue of $T_R^*T_R$ is $\mu_n=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$, each with multiplicity two. For the inverse sequence model, order the cosine–sine modes by nonincreasing multiplier $t_n$, breaking ties by frequency and then placing cosine before sine; write the resulting ordered singular values as $(s_j)$ and their squares as $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Such an ordering exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes exceed any positive threshold. Use the Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ and its continuous geometric-variance candidate grid in the SOLIT rule with known $\sigma>0$.
before.strategy: Verify the mean-zero gradiometry spectrum, ordered Tikhonov filter and continuous geometric-variance grid.

before.title: SOLIT for the periodic heat equation (reported simulation)
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice.

Let the real periodic Fourier coefficient space be $X=Y=\mathbb R\oplus\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, with one constant coordinate and cosine–sine coordinate pairs for each positive frequency, and give it the canonical inner product $\langle(c_0,(a_n,b_n)),(d_0,(c_n,d_n))\rangle=c_0d_0+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. The interleaving map $(c_0,(a_n,b_n))\mapsto(c_0,a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is an isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so this is a real Hilbert space. For a heat time $\bar t>0$, define the periodic heat forward operator by
$$
T_{\bar t}(c_0,(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1})=(c_0,(e^{-n^2\bar t}a_n,e^{-n^2\bar t}b_n)_{n\ge1}).
$$
Its eigenvalues for $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$ are $1$ on the constant mode and $e^{-2n^2\bar t}$ on both modes of frequency $n$. The singular system for the sequence model is ordered as the constant mode, then cosine and sine modes in increasing positive frequency; its singular values are nonincreasing. Use the truth whose function is $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and observe its weak Gaussian white-noise data with known standard deviation $\sigma>0$. Li and Werner report an empirical SOLIT simulation at $\bar t=0.1$ using $10^4$ Monte Carlo runs: they find that SOLIT's rate is very close to the oracle rate, while whether it equals the minimax rate is unclear; the empirical price of adaptation is somewhat irregular, especially for spectral cut-off. These are reported simulation findings, not a theorem or a simulation performed for this library.

For the spectral-cutoff candidate sequence $\alpha_n=e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0$, the variance sums $V_n=1+2\sum_{k=1}^n e^{2k^2\bar t}$ do not have a uniformly bounded consecutive ratio: $V_n/V_{n-1}\to\infty$. Thus this infinite spectral-cutoff sequence does not meet the uniform geometric-variance-grid condition. A continuous Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ does admit such a grid because its variance function is continuous, decreases from $+\infty$ to $0$, and can be sampled at successive fixed variance ratios.
before.strategy: Compute the periodic heat spectrum, verify the Tikhonov filter, show the cutoff grid ratio diverges, and report only the cited simulation.

before.title: Level, power, and weighted regularization of Gaussian MAP feature tests
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,H$ be separable real Hilbert spaces, $K:X\to H$ bounded and linear, $\epsilon>0$, and let $U$ be a Borel Gaussian prior with mean $m_0$ and positive self-adjoint, injective, trace-class covariance $C_0$, independent of a jointly Gaussian centered family $Z$ indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$. Fix $h\in X$, define $S=C_0^{1/2}$, $B=SK^*KS$, $R=(B+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}$, $\Phi_h=KSRSh$, and $c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H-\langle m_0,h\rangle_X$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ and let the raw MAP test reject exactly when $Y_x(\Phi_h)>c_h$. Define $G(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/2}\,ds$, the standard normal cumulative distribution function. For every $x\in X$ its rejection probability is
$$\mathbb P_x\{Y_x(\Phi_h)>c_h\}=\begin{cases}G\!\left(\dfrac{\langle x,K^*\Phi_h\rangle_X-c_h}{\epsilon\|\Phi_h\|_H}\right),&\Phi_h\ne0,\\[6pt]\mathbf1\{0>c_h\},&\Phi_h=0.\end{cases}$$

Let $P_Y$ be the prior-predictive law of the field $Y(g)=\langle KU,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ on $\mathbb R^H$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra, and let $\Pi_y$ and $M_y$ be the data-indexed posterior kernel and mean supplied by the Gaussian posterior-law theorem, using supplied finite or countable complete orthonormal bases of $X$ and $H$ as in that theorem. For every $y$, the scalar feature marginal under $\Pi_y$ is normal with mean $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X$ and variance $\langle C_{\rm post}h,h\rangle_X$; its mode is its mean, with the support point serving as the mode when the variance is zero. For each fixed $h$, the raw MAP test agrees for $P_Y$-almost every $y$ with rejection exactly when this posterior marginal mode is positive. The exceptional null set may depend on $h$. If $h=0$, then $\Phi_h=c_h=0$, and the raw test returns $0$ almost surely under every sampling law and under $P_Y$.

For a further real Hilbert space $V$ and a continuous linear injection $i:V\to X$, define the residual functional $r_\Phi\in V^*$, where $V^*$ is the continuous dual of $V$, by
$$r_\Phi(v)=\langle Ki(v),\Phi\rangle_H-\langle i(v),h\rangle_X,\qquad \|r_\Phi\|_{V^*}=\sup_{\|v\|_V\le1}|r_\Phi(v)|.$$
For $0<\alpha<1$ let $z_{1-\alpha}$ satisfy $G(z_{1-\alpha})=1-\alpha$. If $\Phi\ne0$, the calibrated probe test rejects exactly when
$$Y_x(\Phi)>\epsilon\|\Phi\|_H z_{1-\alpha}+\|r_\Phi\|_{V^*}.$$
Its rejection probability at every $x\in X$ is the same displayed Gaussian-tail formula with $\Phi$ in place of $\Phi_h$ and calibrated threshold in place of $c_h$. If $x=i(v)$ satisfies $\|v\|_V\le1$ and $\langle x,h\rangle_X\le0$, this test has rejection probability at most $\alpha$. For $\Phi=0$ it never rejects and has level zero.

As an additional weighted-regularization identity, assume Countable Choice and suppose that $C_0K^*K=K^*KC_0$. Let $J$ be the real partial isometry in the polar decomposition $K=J(K^*K)^{1/2}$. Let $\mathcal D=\{C_0^{1/2}x:x\in X\}$, and define $C_0^{-1/2}$ as the inverse of $C_0^{1/2}$ on $\mathcal D$. On $\Psi\in H$, set
$$J_h(\Psi)=\|K^*\Psi-h\|_X^2+\epsilon^2\|C_0^{-1/2}J^*\Psi\|_X^2$$
when $J^*\Psi\in\mathcal D$, and set $J_h(\Psi)=+\infty$ otherwise. Then $\Phi_h$ is a minimizer of $J_h$, and
$$K^*\Phi_h=B(B+\epsilon^2I_X)^{-1}h.$$
before.strategy: Derive raw and calibrated power from scalar normal tails, then minimize the weighted objective in a common eigenbasis.

before.title: A compact diagonal map has a closure-only feature
before.statement: Assume Countable Choice. On the real Hilbert space $X=H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, define $Kx=(x_j/j)_{j\ge1}$ and the feature vector $h=(1/j)_{j\ge1}$. Fix $\epsilon>0$, let $Z$ be a jointly Gaussian centered family indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$, and define $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$. The map $K$ is compact and self-adjoint. Its adjoint range contains every finitely supported sequence, so $\overline{R(K^*)}=\ell^2$. The vector $h$ belongs to $\ell^2$ but not to $R(K^*)$, since any preimage would have all coordinates equal to $1$. Thus this feature lies in the closure of the adjoint range but is not exactly estimable by one probe.
before.strategy: Approximate the diagonal map by finite-rank truncations and compare the dense adjoint range with the chosen feature.

before.definition: For a finite-tree probe design $\mathcal C=((C_d,N_d))_{d=1}^D$, a receiver $r\in R$ is **covered** if $r\in C_d$ for some $d$. For a nonroot internal vertex $v$, a design $C_d$ **splits** $v$ if there are distinct children $c,c'$ of $v$ and receivers $r,s\in C_d$ such that $r$ lies in the subtree rooted at $c$ and $s$ lies in the subtree rooted at $c'$. The design satisfies the **split/coverage condition** if every receiver is covered and every nonroot internal vertex is split by at least one design.

The observed log likelihood is
$$

with $\ell(p)=-\infty$ if any positive-count pattern has zero probability.

$$

$$

before.title: Small-ball MAP conventions and Cameron–Martin relative modes
before.statement:
Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

before.title: Posterior contraction rate in a Gaussian sequence inverse experiment
before.statement:
Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

after.title: Posterior contraction rate in a Gaussian sequence inverse experiment
after.statement:
Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

before.title: Exact posterior second moment and contraction bound for a Gaussian sequence inverse problem
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

before.title: Exact adaptive credible coverage by posterior-null deletion
before.statement:
Assume AC and Countable Choice. Fix $p>0$, $C\ge1$, $0<\beta_-<\beta_+<A<\infty$, $R\ge1$, $L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, $\rho\ge2$, $m\in(0,R]$, and $0<\gamma<1$. Let a known positive singular-value sequence satisfy $C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, and observe $X_i=\kappa_i\theta_i+n^{-1/2}\xi_i$ for $i\ge1$, where the fixed truth $\theta=(\theta_i)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ and the $\xi_i$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. For $\alpha>0$, use the product prior $\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha})$ and its product Gaussian posterior with coordinate mean $n\kappa_iX_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$ and variance $(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)^{-1}$. Select $\widehat\alpha_n$ as a Borel global maximizer over $[0,A]$ of the marginal log-likelihood score
$$\ell_n(\alpha;X)=-\frac12\sum_{i\ge1}\left[\log\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right)-\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2X_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}\right],$$
assuming the score series is finite on a Borel data domain of probability one for the truths below and is upper semicontinuous in $\alpha$ there. The $\widehat\alpha_n=0$ branch uses the whole space $\ell^2$ and asserts no posterior probability on $\ell^2$.

For $\theta\in\ell^2$, write $\|\theta\|_2=(\sum_{i\ge1}\theta_i^2)^{1/2}$. For $B\subseteq\ell^2$, define $\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(B)=\sup_{u,v\in B}\|u-v\|_2$, with $\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(\varnothing)=0$.

For $\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]$, let $\Theta_\beta(R)=\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{i\ge1}i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le R^2\}$ and let $\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consist of those $\theta\in\ell^2$ satisfying $\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2\le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2$ for every integer $N\ge N_0$. Put $\mathcal G_\beta=\Theta_\beta(R)\cap\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\cap\{\theta:\theta_1=0,\ \|\theta\|_2\ge m\}$ and assume the fixed constants make each $\mathcal G_\beta$ nonempty. There exists a single graph-measurable data-indexed set rule $C_{n,\gamma}(X)\subseteq\ell^2$, depending only on the known model and class constants and not on $\theta$ or $\beta$, such that on $\widehat\alpha_n>0$ it has posterior mass $\Pi_{\widehat\alpha_n}(C_{n,\gamma}(X)\mid X)\ge1-\gamma$, its uniform frequentist coverage satisfies
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}\left|P_\theta^{(n)}\{\theta\in C_{n,\gamma}(X)\}-(1-\gamma)\right|\longrightarrow0,$$
and its $\ell^2$-diameter has the no-log rate $n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$ uniformly in the following sense: for every $\eta>0$ there is $K_\eta<\infty$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}P_\theta^{(n)}\left\{\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(C_{n,\gamma}(X))>K_\eta n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}\right\}\le\eta.$$

references.locator: Theorem 3.6 and §5 supply conservative inflated-ball coverage; model §§2–3. The posterior-null deletion construction and compact-beta uniform diameter argument here are local deductions from the stated local suppliers, not attributed to this article.

before.strategy: Construct a conservatively covering inflated empirical-Bayes ball, delete the posterior-null truth hyperplane outside a Gaussian event of exact nominal probability, and prove uniform Sobolev diameter via the lower-selector bracket.

before.title: A Gaussian pCN kernel leaves a normal posterior invariant
before.statement:
Let $H=\mathbb R$, give the unknown parameter $u$ the prior law
$\mu_0=N(0,1)$, and observe one datum $Y=0$ from the model
$Y\mid u\sim N(u,1)$. The Gaussian conjugate update gives posterior
$\mu=N(0,1/2)$. Use the potential $\Phi(u)=u^2/2$ in the pCN algorithm. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$, propose
$v=\rho u+\beta\xi$ with $\xi\sim N(0,1)$ independent of the current
state, and accept with probability
$$\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp((u^2-v^2)/2)\}.$$
The resulting pCN probability kernel leaves $N(0,1/2)$ invariant for every
$\beta\in[0,1]$.

before.title: Posterior computation error budget
before.statement:
Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

before.title: Population regression and exact-flow meaning of conditional flow matching
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $\eta$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $\pi$ be a proper Bayesian joint law on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ with data marginal $\pi_Y$ and posterior-kernel version $\pi_y$. Assume $\int|x_0|^2\eta(dx_0)+\int|x_1|^2\pi(dx_1,dy)<\infty$. Let $t$, $X_0$ and $(X_1,Y)$ be independent with law $\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\otimes\eta\otimes\pi$, where $X_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1$, and $V=X_1-X_0$ has finite second moment. Write $\mathcal L(v):=\mathbb E|v(t,X_t,Y)-V|^2$ and let $\widehat{\mathcal L}_n(v)$ be the empirical mean of this squared residual over $n\ge1$ independent training triples. Then the conditional-expectation class $v^*(t,X_t,Y)=\mathbb E[V\mid\sigma(t,X_t,Y)]$ admits a measurable representative in $(t,x,y)$ and uniquely minimizes $\mathcal L$ over square-integrable predictors measurable in these coordinates, up to almost-sure equality. For every fixed measurable candidate $v$ with finite population loss,
$$\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathcal L}_n(v)]=\mathcal L(v).$$
This expectation identity is for a fixed candidate, not a data-dependent fitted field.

If a fitted field satisfies all hypotheses of the global ODE flow lemma, it has an exact triangular terminal map $T(x,y)=(T_y(x),y)$. If also $T_{\#}(\eta\otimes\pi_Y)=\pi$, then $T_y{}_{\#}\eta=\pi_y$ as probability measures outside one $\pi_Y$-null set. These conclusions make no assertion that finite training or numerical solver success establishes the exact joint pushforward identity.

before.title: Accurate posterior means with low independent-MH acceptance
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the general density-based Metropolis–Hastings interface. In the stationary-diffusion inverse-problem experiment with $m=256$ observations, noise variance $\gamma^2=10^{-5}$, and $n_{KL}=128$ prior modes, use the baseline conditional-flow-matching MLP with 800 hidden units. The reported flow-matching independent-Metropolis–Hastings acceptance rates for four different true parameters are respectively $0.66\%$, $11.21\%$, $5.97\%$, and $5.47\%$. In this same experiment, the reported posterior means and 95\% bands agree with the DRAM reference to between $0.8\%$ and $1.8\%$ in relative $L^2$. The first truth is a prior-predictive tail observation: its normalized radius is $2.53$, the median training radius is $0.85$, and only $0.12\%$ of the two million training observations have a larger radius. This reported case shows that close posterior means and bands do not by themselves imply high independent-Metropolis–Hastings acceptance or establish full posterior accuracy.

before.title: Besov smoothness gives the exact collared Sobolev penalty a cutoff source bound

references.title: Frederic Weidling, Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs
references.locator: Theorem 6.12; the present proof treats the intrinsic quadratic Sobolev pairing directly

before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Let $B^r_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ have norm $\sup_{j\ge0}2^{jr}\|\mathbf1_{A_j}\widehat f\|_2$, where $A_0=\{|\xi|<2\}$ and $A_j=\{2^j\le|\xi|<2^{j+1}\}$ for $j\ge1$; the restriction space on $\Omega$ consists of restrictions of members of this whole-space Besov space.

Let $\sigma^\dagger\in H^s(\Omega)\cap B^t_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ be real and equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus B_\rho$. Then there is $C>0$, depending on $\sigma^\dagger,s,t,\rho$, such that for every real $\sigma\in H^s(\Omega)$ also equal to $1$ there and every integer $J\ge0$,
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le C2^{J(2s-t-1)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-J(t-s)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}.$$
Consequently, suppose on a specified admissible sublevel a forward map $G$ satisfies $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_0\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $0\le\omega\le1$. For the exact regularizer $R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, its exact Bregman distance is $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\frac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, and
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le\frac34D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)+C_1\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)^{2(t-s)/(t-1)}.$$
In particular, an $H^1$ stability modulus of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-(s-3/2)}$ yields a VSC source term of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}$ with $\nu=(t-s)(2s-3)/(t-1)$. The conditional stability estimate is a hypothesis here, not a conclusion.

before.title: Collared Sobolev conductivities have regular Liouville potentials and H1 recovery

references.title: Frederic Weidling, Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs
references.locator: Lemmas 6.4–6.5 and the potential-to-conductivity estimate (6.9)

before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Then $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$ and $\log g_j$ belong to $C^1$, with $g_j-1,\log g_j\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and $C^1$. The real Liouville potentials
$$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

before.title: Source corrections for three-dimensional EIT rates

references.title: Barbara Kaltenbacher, Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography, Section 3, Theorem 10 and Corollary 11
Frederic Weidling, Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs, Chapter 6, Theorems 6.10–6.15
Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Chapter 10, Theorem 10.7

before.statement:
Kaltenbacher's 2024 paper treats the three-dimensional unit ball with background conductivity $\sigma_{\rm bg}\equiv1$, quadratic penalty $\check R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{H^{s_1}(\Omega)}^2$, $s_1\in(5/2,7/2)$, and truth $\sigma^\dagger\in B^{s_2}_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ for $s_2\in(s_1,2s_1-1)$. Its Theorem 10 reports a logarithmic VSC exponent

$$\nu_{\rm paper}:=\frac{(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)}{s_1-1},$$

with $b=3/4$, and Corollary 11 reports a conductivity-norm rate using that exponent divided by the source parameter $\widetilde p$ for the joint, split, and frozen-Newton methods. These printed formulas are source assertions; the locally proved EIT conclusions use the corrected exponent and parameter qualifications below.

The cited Weidling Theorem 6.15 at $p=2$ gives denominator $s_2-1$ in the corresponding logarithmic exponent. In addition, the quadratic Bregman distance is one half the squared $H^{s_1}$ norm error, so a Bregman rate with logarithmic exponent $\nu$ yields a norm exponent $\nu/2$; this abstract implication alone does not supply every exponent reported by Corollary 11. The sufficient parameter coupling in the abstract rate theorem requires $\alpha H(c/\alpha)\asymp\delta^2$ for a fixed $c>0$. For a logarithmic index with $H(q)\asymp(\log q)^{-\nu}$, no pure-power choice $\alpha\asymp\delta^{\widetilde p}$ with $0<\widetilde p\le2$ satisfies this two-sided coupling. Kaltenbacher's Remark 1 separately asserts that pure powers still give the same logarithmic rate; that separate assertion needs an independent derivation and is not ruled out solely by failure of the sufficient coupling. The local joint and frozen EIT theorems assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, use the corrected exponent $\nu=(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)/(s_2-1)$, retain the entire stated Sobolev/Besov truth range, and prove the conductivity norm exponent $\nu/2$. They give balanced parameters, every strict pure power $0<\widetilde p<2$, and the nominal endpoint $\widetilde p=2$ with an explicit stronger actual-noise condition. The universal abstract endpoint assertion under arbitrary deterministic noise bounded only by $\delta$ is false, as shown by the exact quadratic counterexample in the endpoint lemma; that example does not claim to be an EIT-specific counterexample.

The local application uses mean-zero Neumann currents and boundary-mean-zero Neumann states. Its data space is the centered sequence $(\mathscr N_\sigma-\mathscr N_1)Y_{\ell k}$ in $\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$, or equivalently the corresponding affine translate for absolute voltages. This centering is necessary: at the background conductivity $1$, the uncentered voltage columns have norms $1/\ell$ with multiplicity $2\ell+1$, so their squared sum diverges. The centered Neumann-map differentiability, $H^1$ logarithmic stability, exact intrinsic Sobolev/Besov source inequality, augmented factorization and inverse, frozen Taylor estimate, and regularizer/penalty compatibility now have local proofs. The stability proof retains the Fourier modulation in the CGO remainder and integrates its negative-Sobolev norm before absorption; it does not use the invalid unmodulated pointwise inference in the printed Weidling proof.

before.title: Loomis–Whitney integral inequality
before.statement: Let $n\ge2$. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $g_i:\mathbb R^{n-1}\to[0,\infty)$ be Lebesgue-measurable and integrable, with its arguments identified with all coordinates except $x_i$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_n)^{1/(n-1)}\,dx\le\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g_i\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

before.title: Dual attainment and convergence of TV source certificates
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be one of the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann TV functionals. Assume that $R$ is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous, and that $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-$R$ exact solution of $Au=f$ with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Define $K:=\{p\in Y:A^*p\in\partial R(0)\}$ and $D_{\alpha,w}(p):=\langle f+w,p\rangle_Y-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p\|_Y^2$ for $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$.

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. If $u_{\alpha,w}$ is any supplied global minimizer of $u\mapsto\frac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)$, then $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(0)$. For every such supplied minimizer, the correctly normalized primal-dual value identity is

$$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

Barbara Kaltenbacher, Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3
Jonathan M. Borwein and Jon D. Vanderwerff, Convex Functions: Constructions, Characterizations and Counterexamples, Exercise 4.4.1

references.locator: §6, Definition 6.1, printed p. 37, for local distribution pairings and cotangent coordinates.

before.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

before.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.

before.statement:
Let $R$ be an analytic double-fibration transform, and fix a relation point $(z_0,\zeta_0;x_0,\xi_0)$ at which $d\pi_L$ is injective. For distributions $u$ supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $x_0$, data Gaussian exponential regularity at $(z_0,\zeta_0)$ implies object Gaussian exponential regularity at $(x_0,\xi_0)$.

More precisely, for data parameters $v=(q,p)$ near that point on the local embedded image $V$ of $\pi_L$, write $\chi(v)=(X(v),\Xi(v))$ for the paired object covector. The transpose localized data Gaussian has the form
$$
K_\lambda(x,v)=\lambda^{-d/2}e^{i\lambda\psi(x,v)}A(x,v;\lambda)+E_\lambda(x,v), \qquad d=\dim Z-\dim X,
$$
where $A$ is an elliptic classical analytic amplitude, $E_\lambda=O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative, and
$$
\psi(X(v),v)=-q\cdot p,\quad d_x\psi(X(v),v)=-\Xi(v),\quad \operatorname{Im}\psi(x,v)\ge c|x-X(v)|^2
$$
for real parameters. The map $\chi$ is an analytic submersion onto an open object cotangent neighborhood and has a local analytic section there. The constant factor in the kernel formula includes the nonzero Gaussian determinant on its continuous branch.

where $A$ is an elliptic classical analytic amplitude, $E_\lambda=O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative, and
$$
\psi(X(v),v)=-q\cdot p,\quad d_x\psi(X(v),v)=-\Xi(v),\quad \operatorname{Im}\psi(x,v)\ge c|x-X(v)|^2

before.title: Finite propagation for the wave equation on a Riemannian manifold

references.title: Medet Nursultanov and Lauri Oksanen, Introduction to inverse problems for hyperbolic PDEs (full lecture notes, arXiv:2311.06020v2)

references.title: Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis (full author lecture notes, arXiv:2312.08123v1)
references.locator: Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Remark 3.3, PDF pp. 21–22: static-potential ray transform, uniqueness, and the finite-time support threshold; the local Riemannian energy estimate is proved here.

before.statement:
Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and define the intrinsic distance $d_g(x,y)$ as the infimum of Riemannian lengths of piecewise $C^1$ curves in $M$ from $x$ to $y$. For a nonempty set $K\subseteq M$, write $d_g(x,K)=\inf_{y\in K}d_g(x,y)$; for nonempty sets $A,B\subseteq M$, write $d_g(A,B)=\inf_{a\in A,b\in B}d_g(a,b)$. Let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time; the solution functions may be real- or complex-valued. Set
$$L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q(x),\qquad \Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g.$$
For a smooth solution $u$ up to the boundary on $[0,T]\times M$, let $u_0=u(0,\cdot)$, $u_1=\partial_tu(0,\cdot)$, and let $h=u|_{[0,T]\times\partial M}$ be its Dirichlet boundary value. The support of a function is the closure of the set where it is nonzero.

(i) If $h=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}u_0\cup\operatorname{supp}u_1\subseteq K$ for a nonempty closed $K\subseteq M$, then
$$\operatorname{supp}u(t,\cdot)\subseteq\{x\in M:d_g(x,K)\le t\}\qquad(0\le t\le T).$$

(ii) If $u_0=u_1=0$ and $h(t,\cdot)=0$ for $0\le t\le s_0$ with $0\le s_0<T$, then
$$\operatorname{supp}u(t,\cdot)\subseteq\{x\in M:d_g(x,\partial M)\le t-s_0\}\qquad(s_0\le t\le T).$$
The same assertion holds backward in time for a smooth solution with zero terminal data and boundary value vanishing for $s_1\le t\le T$, with $0\le t\le s_1$ and $t-s_0$ replaced by $s_1-t$.

(iii) Let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be time independent, put $Q=\operatorname{supp}(q_1-q_2)$, and suppose $Q\ne\varnothing$ and $d_g(Q,\partial M)>T/2$. If $u$ solves $L_{q_1}u=0$ with zero initial data and smooth boundary value compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\partial M$, and $v$ solves $L_{q_2}v=0$ with zero terminal data and smooth boundary value compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\partial M$, then
$$\int_0^T\!\int_M(q_1-q_2)u(t,x)v(t,x)\,dV_g(x)\,dt=0.$$
This is the two-boundary-trip finite-time invisibility statement at the level of the interior pairing.

before.title: Gaussian beams concentrated on an embedded null bicharacteristic
before.proof_strategy: complex phase, Riccati transport, Borel summation, and energy correction

references.title: Lauri Oksanen, Mikko Salo, Plamen Stefanov, and Gunther Uhlmann, Inverse problems for real principal type operators (arXiv:2001.07599v2)
references.locator: §3, Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 21 and proof through PDF p. 33: endpoint-localized residual, transported mass, phase, Riccati positivity, transport, Borel realization and patching. The no-cusp local phase argument is supplied below.

references.title: Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis (full author lecture notes, arXiv:2312.08123v1)
references.locator: §3.4, PDF pp. 32–39: Gaussian-beam construction sketch and its explicit proof boundary.

before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a smooth spacetime manifold of dimension $m\ge2$ with a smooth positive density, and let $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ be a scalar second-order differential operator with smooth coefficients in local coordinates. In each local chart, use the microlocal convention $D_j:=(1/i)\partial_{x_j}=-i\partial_{x_j}$ and $D^\alpha:=D_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots D_m^{\alpha_m}$. Its principal symbol $p(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=2}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$ is real and satisfies $dp\ne0$ on $\{p=0\}\subset T^*X\setminus0$. Equip $T^*X$ with its canonical cotangent symplectic form and define the Hamilton vector field by $\iota_{H_p}\omega_{\rm can}=dp$. A null bicharacteristic is a nonzero integral curve of $H_p$ contained in $\{p=0\}$. Let $\Gamma$ be a compact phase-space segment that is an injective immersion with no repeated phase points; assume its base projection is an immersion (the no-cusp condition) and that the segment is contained in the interior of $T^*X\setminus0$. For every integer $N\ge1$, there are complex smooth functions $u_\lambda$ formed from finitely many branch-local packets, each supported in a fixed tubular neighborhood of an embedded local branch of the base projection of $\Gamma$. Their longitudinal cutoffs equal one on the portion under observation and are supported in the chosen branch extensions. As $\lambda\to+\infty$, they have the following properties:

1. On each embedded local branch of the base projection, the phase has a formal transverse Taylor expansion solving the complex eikonal equation to every prescribed finite order; its transverse imaginary Hessian is positive definite and yields Gaussian decay away from that branch. At projected crossings the beam is the finite sum of the branch-local packets; a single phase on the crossing union is not required.
2. On each branch the amplitudes solve the transport hierarchy to the corresponding order and are realized by a Borel sum; the finitely many branch-local packets are patched and summed using their compatible jets.
3. Write $s$ for a fixed smooth parameter on the projected curve and fix its origin. There is a smooth positive transported density $w(s)ds$, normalized by $w(0)=1$, such that the measures $|u_\lambda|^2dV_X$ converge against compactly supported smooth tests away from endpoint neighborhoods to $\int a(\pi\Gamma(s))w(s)ds$. The weight is the one determined by the leading transport equation; a general operator with complex lower-order coefficients need not give constant $w$. For the real formally self-adjoint wave operator, with parameter equal to physical time along a unit-speed spatial ray and the wave phase normalized by $|\partial_t\phi|=1$, the transport gives $w=1$.
4. For every compact set $K$ disjoint from neighborhoods of the two projected endpoints, $\|Pu_\lambda\|_{L^2(K)}=O(\lambda^{-N})$ for each requested $N$, after carrying the expansions sufficiently far. The endpoint cutoff generally produces a residual near those endpoints. In particular, if the segment extends outside a compact measurement domain and its two endpoint neighborhoods are disjoint from that domain, the residual has the asserted order throughout that domain.

The cutoff in the ambient extension is one along the portion of the ray under observation and vanishes beyond the extended endpoints. A segment wholly in the spacetime interior does not have a globally negligible endpoint residual. Its tube can be supported away from the boundary and then has zero boundary trace; a wave beam entering and exiting a measurement domain instead has its actual smooth boundary trace there. In this wave specialization, if the extended beam is zero near the required initial or terminal time, the zero-boundary energy correction on the measurement cylinder gives an exact solution with the same boundary data and an $O(\lambda^{-N})$ energy error for any requested $N$. The claim concerns an embedded segment in phase space and permits projected self-intersections.

before.statement:
Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold, let $T>0$, and let $Q=(0,T)\times M$ carry product measure $dV_gdt$. Fix a unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$ and $t_0$ with $0<t_0<T-L$, and set $\Gamma(s)=(t_0+s,\gamma(s))$, $0\le s\le L$; $ds$ denotes its arclength parameter. Let $a\in C^\infty([0,T]\times M)$, and for each $\lambda\ge1$ let $u_{j,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\in L^2(Q)$ and $R_{j,\lambda}\in L^2(Q)$ for $j=1,2$. Suppose $\|u_{j,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_0$, $\|R_{j,\lambda}\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_1\lambda^{-1/2}$, and
$$\int_Q a\,u_{1,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}u_{2,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\,dV_gdt\longrightarrow \int_0^L a(t_0+s,\gamma(s))\,ds.$$
Set $u_{j,\lambda}=u_{j,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}+R_{j,\lambda}$. Then
$$\left|\int_Q a\,u_{1,\lambda}u_{2,\lambda}\,dV_gdt-\int_Q a\,u_{1,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}u_{2,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\,dV_gdt\right|=O(\lambda^{-1/2}),$$
and hence the exact-solution product has the same ray-integral limit. The real self-adjoint wave application is to beams satisfying the following additional supplier conditions: the observed ray has a compact embedded phase-space extension with immersed base projection; its two endpoint cutoff neighborhoods lie outside the measurement cylinder; and the approximate forward beam vanishes near $t=0$, while the approximate terminal beam vanishes near $t=T$. These temporal vanishing conditions are separate from the location of the spatial endpoint residuals. Use physical time along the unit-speed spatial ray and the normalization $|\partial_t\phi|=1$, with initial transported mass one. Then the Gaussian-beam lemma gives the unweighted ray measure and residual $O(\lambda^{-N})$ throughout $Q$. Apply the wave energy wellposedness theorem with zero boundary data and zero initial data for the forward correction, or zero terminal data for the terminal correction, to the negative residual. Since $\|Pu_{j,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le\sqrt T\|Pu_{j,\lambda}^{\mathrm{app}}\|_{L^2(Q)}$, its energy estimate gives an $L^2(Q)$ correction $O(\lambda^{-N})$, hence the assumed $O(\lambda^{-1/2})$ order after choosing $N\ge1$. The exact waves retain the actual approximate boundary traces. This application asserts no temporal vanishing merely from an extension outside the measurement domain; the generic error estimate above only needs its explicitly stated norm and product-limit hypotheses.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be time independent. Put $Q_0=\operatorname{supp}(q_1-q_2)$, the closure of the set on which $q_1-q_2$ is nonzero, and suppose $Q_0\ne\varnothing$ and $d_g(Q_0,\partial M)>T/2$, where $d_g$ is the intrinsic Riemannian distance. For every smooth Dirichlet input $h\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\partial M)$, the full time-dependent forward Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps satisfy
$$\Lambda_{q_1}^+h=\Lambda_{q_2}^+h\quad\text{in }L^2((0,T)\times\partial M,dS_gdt).$$
Thus a perturbation supported farther than half the observation time from the boundary cannot be detected by boundary measurements made before time $T$.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$

$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

before.title: Anisotropic conductivity and weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map

references.title: Mikko Salo, The Calderón problem on Riemannian manifolds (2012)

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

before.title: A boundary-fixing diffeomorphism preserves the anisotropic DN map

references.title: Mikko Salo, The Calderón problem on Riemannian manifolds (2012)
Thierry Daudé, Niky Kamran, and François Nicoleau, A survey of non-uniqueness results for the anisotropic Calderón problem with disjoint data (2018)

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, hence Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected domain with smooth boundary, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite. Let $F:\overline\Omega\to\overline\Omega$ be a diffeomorphism smooth through the boundary, with smooth inverse and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=\operatorname{id}$. For $x=F(y)$, put $J_F(y)=|\det DF(y)|$ and define

$$ (F_*\gamma)(x)=\frac{DF(y)\,\gamma(y)\,DF(y)^T}{J_F(y)},\qquad y=F^{-1}(x). $$

Then $F_*\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite matrix conductivity and its weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map equals that of $\gamma$. Explicitly, for every pair of boundary trace-data classes $f,h\in\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$,

$$\langle\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle,$$

where each map is the weak energy form $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, $u_{\gamma,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$, and $V_h$ is any $H^1$ representative of $h$.

The same gauge invariance has a Riemannian form. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, $g$ a smooth Riemannian metric, $\Gamma\subseteq\partial M$ relatively open, and $\Phi:M\to M$ a smooth diffeomorphism with $\Phi|_\Gamma=\operatorname{id}$. Define $(\Phi^*g)_p(v,w):=g_{\Phi(p)}(D\Phi_pv,D\Phi_pw)$. The cotangent inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_g$ is induced by $g^{-1}$, and in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det(g_{ij})}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. A smooth function $u$ is $g$-harmonic when $\int_M\langle du,d\psi\rangle_g\,dV_g=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$. Then $u\circ\Phi$ is $\Phi^*g$-harmonic; for any two smooth $g$-harmonic functions $u,v$,

$$\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g.$$

If the boundary traces of $u,v$ are supported in $\Gamma$, then composition by $\Phi$ leaves both traces fixed, so the local energy measurement of every such smooth harmonic pair is unchanged. In particular, if for each $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ the Dirichlet solutions for $g$ and $\Phi^*g$ with trace $f$ are unique and smooth, then the corresponding local energy DN maps agree.

before.axiom_use: Countable Choice is assumed only for the contextual infinite-dimensional Picard statement. The finite matrix instructions themselves use finite data and no choice principle.
before.statement:
**Inputs and admissible conditions.** Fix the domain $D$, wavenumber $k>0$, and library Fourier convention from the fixed-frequency data definition. Give nonempty finite lists of incident directions $d_1,\ldots,d_s\in S^2$ and observation directions $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\in S^2$. Give a finite measurable partition $D=\bigsqcup_{n=1}^N E_n$ with $|E_n|>0$, complex Born-data samples $y=(y_{ba})\in\mathbb C^{rs}$, a discrepancy threshold $\delta\ge0$, and an iteration budget $B\in\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The sample frequency for pair $(\theta_b,d_a)$ is $\xi_{ba}:=k(\theta_b-d_a)/(2\pi)$. The declared finite discrete Born Fourier matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{rs\times N}$ has entries
$$F_{(b,a),n}:=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{E_n}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi_{ba}}\,dx.$$
For a piecewise-constant contrast $q_c:=\sum_{n=1}^N c_n1_{E_n}$, its sampled first Born data vector is exactly $Fc$.
The input also declares a reduced singular-value decomposition
$$Fc=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sigma_j\langle c,v_j\rangle u_j\qquad(c\in\mathbb C^N),$$
where $p=\operatorname{rank}F$, the positive singular values $\sigma_j$ have orthonormal right vectors $v_j$ and orthonormal left vectors $u_j$, and the empty sum is used when $F=0$. Give a scalar filter $g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ whose values at the $\sigma_j$ are finite and with $g(0)=0$. The threshold filter $g_\tau(\sigma)=1/\sigma$ for $\sigma>\tau$ and $g_\tau(\sigma)=0$ for $0\le\sigma\le\tau$ is the truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau\ge0$.

**Instructions and outputs.**

1. If $B=0$, return no estimate, no residual, and status **budget-exhausted**, with zero filter applications.
2. If $B\ge1$, form the coefficient estimate
   $$\widehat c:=\sum_{j:\sigma_j>0}g(\sigma_j)\langle y,u_j\rangle v_j,$$
   where $\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_\ell z_\ell\overline{w_\ell}$ is linear in its first argument. Return the piecewise-constant reconstruction $\widehat q:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\widehat c_n1_{E_n}$ after exactly one filter application.
3. Compute the finite data residual $R:=\|F\widehat c-y\|_2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\sum_\ell|z_\ell|^2)^{1/2}$. Return status **discrepancy** when $R\le\delta$, and **residual-above-threshold** when $R>\delta$; in either case also return $\widehat q$, $R$, and the application count $1$.

This procedure only defines one filtered finite-dimensional Born reconstruction and a residual status. The residual is not an exact-range test for an infinite-dimensional compact forward operator and does not establish a nonlinear solution, identifiability, stability, convergence, or correctness of the reconstructed contrast.
