references.title: Hannes Meinlschmidt, Optimization with Partial Differential Equations, complete lecture notes
Michael Hinze, A Variational Discretization Concept in Control Constrained Optimization: The Linear-Quadratic Case
Fernando Gaspoz, Christian Kreuzer, Andreas Veeser, and Winnifried Wollner, A Posteriori Error Analysis for Optimization with PDE Constraints

before.statement:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ of $\Omega$, and unisolvent reference finite elements assembled on that mesh. Thus the mesh is a finite face-to-face cover by nondegenerate affine simplices with disjoint interiors, and each local finite-element degree-of-freedom map is bijective on its polynomial space. Fix coefficient spaces $\Theta_h=\mathbb R^m$, $V_h=\mathbb R^n$, and $Y_h=\mathbb R^s$ with their standard Euclidean inner products, where $m,n,s\ge1$. Let $Q_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $O_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be open with $Q_h\subseteq O_h$.

A **finite-element PDE model** in this contract consists of a continuously differentiable residual map $R_h:O_h\times V_h\to V_h$ and a continuously differentiable observation map $G_h:O_h\times V_h\to Y_h$. It must supply a continuously differentiable state branch $S_h:O_h\to V_h$ satisfying $R_h(q,S_h(q))=0$ for every $q\in O_h$. For every $q\in Q_h$, this branch must be the specified unique admissible state and the matrix $D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))$ must be invertible. The discrete forward map is $F_h(q):=G_h(q,S_h(q))$. The unisolvent finite-element degrees of freedom identify $V_h$ with its coefficient space; all matrix transposes below are in the fixed Euclidean coefficient inner products.

For data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, reference parameter $q_0\in\Theta_h$, and $\alpha>0$, the discrete nonlinear Tikhonov objective is
$$
\Phi_h(q):=\frac12\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2\qquad(q\in Q_h).
$$
Define the finite-dimensional objective before eliminating the state by
$$
J_h(q,u):=\frac12\|G_h(q,u)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2.
$$
The symbols $\nabla_uJ_h$ and $\nabla_qJ_h$ denote the Euclidean gradient vectors representing the two partial derivative functionals. At an admissible $q$, the **exact discrete adjoint** $p_h(q)\in V_h$ is the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q)=\nabla_uJ_h(q,S_h(q)).
$$
The associated discrete-adjoint gradient vector is
$$
g_h(q):=\nabla_qJ_h(q,S_h(q))-\bigl(D_qR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q).
$$
The next lemma proves that this vector is the gradient of $\Phi_h$; the definition itself asserts no minimizer exists and no gradient iteration converges.

An **admissibility predicate** is a specified finite-time test $\operatorname{adm}_h(q)$ that decides whether $q\in Q_h$ and checks the model's stated coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step hypotheses before a PDE solve. For an explicit time discretization, a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition (CFL condition) is a method-specific bound relating the time step to the mesh and the discrete evolution operator; no universal CFL threshold is part of this definition. A true predicate result certifies that the declared model hypotheses hold for that input, not merely that a heuristic check passed.

The model must also supply an exact finite-dimensional projection routine which returns $P_{Q_h}(z)$ for a queried $z\in\Theta_h$ in finite time or reports failure only when its declared finite call budget is exhausted. The unique nearest point exists because $Q_h$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, but an operational routine for computing it is an additional part of this contract.

A solver routine with declared nonnegative state and adjoint tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and a finite solve budget must return either `failure` or approximate state and adjoint vectors $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$ together with certified finite bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p,\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$. The residual bounds have the exact-system meaning $\|R_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_u$ and $\|(D_uR_h(q,u))^T\widetilde p-\nabla_uJ_h(q,u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_p$, where $u=S_h(q)$; both must satisfy $\rho_u\le\tau_u$ and $\rho_p\le\tau_p$. In particular, an adjoint residual evaluated at $\widetilde u$ alone does not certify $\rho_p$ unless the model also bounds the resulting state and derivative-data defects. With $u=S_h(q)$ and $p=p_h(q)$, the model must certify
$$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\qquad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\qquad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{\Theta_h}\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\qquad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. It then returns
$$
\widetilde g:=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p,\qquad \widetilde F:=G_h(q,\widetilde u),
$$
All constants and state/adjoint error bounds must be justified for the chosen model with every derivative-data, geometry, quadrature, and algebraic-solve defect retained. Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ of $\Omega$, and unisolvent reference finite elements assembled on that mesh. Thus the mesh is a finite face-to-face cover by nondegenerate affine simplices with disjoint interiors, and each local finite-element degree-of-freedom map is bijective on its finite-dimensional shape-function space. Fix coefficient spaces $\Theta_h=\mathbb R^m$, $V_h=\mathbb R^n$, and $Y_h=\mathbb R^s$ with their standard Euclidean inner products, where $m,n,s\ge1$. Let $Q_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $O_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be open with $Q_h\subseteq O_h$.

A **finite-element PDE model** in this contract consists of a continuously differentiable residual map $R_h:O_h\times V_h\to V_h$ and a continuously differentiable observation map $G_h:O_h\times V_h\to Y_h$. It must supply a continuously differentiable state branch $S_h:O_h\to V_h$ satisfying $R_h(q,S_h(q))=0$ for every $q\in O_h$. For every $q\in Q_h$, this branch must be the specified unique admissible state and the matrix $D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))$ must be invertible. The discrete forward map is $F_h(q):=G_h(q,S_h(q))$. The unisolvent finite-element degrees of freedom identify $V_h$ with its coefficient space; all matrix transposes below are in the fixed Euclidean coefficient inner products.

For data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, reference parameter $q_0\in\Theta_h$, and $\alpha>0$, the discrete nonlinear Tikhonov objective is
$$
\Phi_h(q):=\frac12\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2\qquad(q\in Q_h).
$$
Define the finite-dimensional objective before eliminating the state by
$$
J_h(q,u):=\frac12\|G_h(q,u)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2.
$$
The symbols $\nabla_uJ_h$ and $\nabla_qJ_h$ denote the Euclidean gradient vectors representing the two partial derivative functionals. At an admissible $q$, the **exact discrete adjoint** $p_h(q)\in V_h$ is the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q)=\nabla_uJ_h(q,S_h(q)).
$$
The associated discrete-adjoint gradient vector is
$$
g_h(q):=\nabla_qJ_h(q,S_h(q))-\bigl(D_qR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q).
$$
The next lemma proves that this vector is the gradient of $\Phi_h$; the definition itself asserts no minimizer exists and no gradient iteration converges.

An **admissibility predicate** is a specified finite-time test $\operatorname{adm}_h(q)$ that decides whether $q\in Q_h$ and checks the model's stated coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step hypotheses before a PDE solve. For an explicit time discretization, a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition (CFL condition) is a method-specific bound relating the time step to the mesh and the discrete evolution operator; no universal CFL threshold is part of this definition. A true predicate result certifies that the declared model hypotheses hold for that input, not merely that a heuristic check passed.

The model must also supply an exact finite-dimensional projection routine which returns $P_{Q_h}(z)$ for a queried $z\in\Theta_h$ in finite time or reports failure only when its declared finite call budget is exhausted. The unique nearest point exists because $Q_h$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, but an operational routine for computing it is an additional part of this contract.

A solver routine with declared nonnegative state and adjoint tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and a finite solve budget must return either `failure` or approximate state and adjoint vectors $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$ together with certified finite bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p,\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$. In particular, an adjoint residual evaluated at $\widetilde u$ alone does not certify $\rho_p$ unless the model also bounds the resulting state and derivative-data defects. $$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\qquad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\qquad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{\Theta_h}\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\qquad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. It then returns
$$
\widetilde g:=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p,\qquad \widetilde F:=G_h(q,\widetilde u),
$$
All constants and state/adjoint error bounds must be justified for the chosen model with every derivative-data, geometry, quadrature, and algebraic-solve defect retained. Certified residual bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p$ do not by themselves imply $\eta_u,\eta_p$; a separate model-valid stability estimate is required. The proposition below derives the resulting $\varepsilon_g$ and $\varepsilon_F$ bounds. Each routine must return within its declared budget or report failure.

If a continuous model $F$ is also supplied, an optional mesh certificate $\varepsilon_{\rm mesh}$ must separately bound the claimed continuous-to-discrete error, such as $\|F_h(q)-F(q)\|$ or $\|\nabla\Phi_h(q)-\nabla\Phi(q)\|$. The state and adjoint algebraic residual certificates do not imply this mesh certificate.

references.title: Michael Hinze, A Variational Discretization Concept in Control Constrained Optimization: The Linear-Quadratic Case

before.statement:
Assume a finite-element PDE model satisfying the admissibility and certificate contract, with nonempty closed convex coefficient set $Q_h$, discrete Tikhonov objective $\Phi_h$ using reference coefficient $q_0$, a state/adjoint solve routine, an exact projection routine, an objective interval routine, and finite solve and evaluation budgets. Let the input be an initial coefficient $q_{\rm init}\in Q_h$, data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, noise bound $\delta\ge0$, penalty $\alpha>0$, state and adjoint residual tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p\ge0$, discrepancy factor $\kappa\ge1$, stationarity tolerance $\tau_g\ge0$, scaling parameter $L>0$, and positive integer budgets $N_{\rm iter}$, $N_{\rm solve}$, $N_{\rm eval}$, and $N_{\rm backtrack}$. The global budget $N_{\rm solve}$ counts state and adjoint solves; $N_{\rm eval}$ counts exact projections and objective-interval evaluations. The scaling parameter $L$ is only a positive step-size scale; it is not assumed to be a Lipschitz constant. The algorithm returns a coefficient, one status from `converged`, `discrepancy-stopped`, `linear-solve-failed`, `inadmissible`, or `budget-exhausted`, and any diagnostics certified at that coefficient.

1. If $q_{\rm init}\notin Q_h$ or the model's exact admissibility predicate is false at $q_{\rm init}$, return status `inadmissible` without solving a PDE. Otherwise set $q:=q_{\rm init}$.

2. For $k=0,\ldots,N_{\rm iter}$, first check the finite-time admissibility predicate, which includes membership in $Q_h$. If it is false, return `inadmissible`. If no global solve or evaluation budget remains, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. Call the state/adjoint solver at $q$ with tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and the remaining solve budget. If it returns `failure`, if either certified residual bound exceeds its declared tolerance, or if any required state/adjoint error estimate or derivative bound is missing or invalid, return `linear-solve-failed`. Otherwise receive $\widetilde g_h$, $\widetilde F_h$, $\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$ and set $\varepsilon_g=(L_{J,u}+L_{R,u}P)\eta_u+M_q\eta_p$ and $\varepsilon_F=L_{G,u}\eta_u$.

4. Use the exact projection routine to compute $P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)$. If the routine fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $\widetilde\rho:=L\|q-P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)\|_2$. If $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g\le\tau_g$, return `converged` with stationarity upper bound $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g$. This status means only that the exact projected-gradient residual of the discrete objective is within tolerance; it is not a claim that an iterate sequence converges or that $q$ is a global minimizer.

5. Compute $d^+:=\|\widetilde F_h-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}+\varepsilon_F$. If $d^+\le\kappa\delta$, return `discrepancy-stopped` with data-residual upper bound $d^+$. This status certifies only the discrete model's data discrepancy.

6. If $k=N_{\rm iter}$, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient with its current diagnostics. Otherwise, evaluate the current objective using its certified interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$. If the evaluation fails because a required state or adjoint solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if the global solve or evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`.

7. For $j=0,\ldots,N_{\rm backtrack}-1$, set $t_j=2^{-j}/L$ and use the exact projection routine to compute $q_j=P_{Q_h}(q-t_j\widetilde g_h)$. If projection fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Reject this trial and continue to the next $j$ if $q_j=q$ or its admissibility predicate is false. Otherwise evaluate a certified interval $[\ell_h(q_j),u_h(q_j)]$. If evaluation fails because a required linear solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if it only exhausts the finite evaluation budget, return `budget-exhausted`. Accept the first trial with $u_h(q_j)\le\ell_h(q)$, set $q:=q_j$, and continue to the next outer iteration.

8. If no trial is accepted within the backtracking budget, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient.

The global solve budget counts all primal and adjoint solves used both at iterates and in objective trials. The evaluation budget counts every projection and objective-interval call. Any continuous-to-discrete mesh bound is reported separately by the model contract and is never inferred from the algebraic state or adjoint residuals.

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega)$ be a real almost-everywhere class with $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$. Set $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with quotient norm $\|[U]\|_{\mathcal D}:=\inf_{w\in H_0^1(\Omega)}\|U+w\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$, and let $\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ be its continuous conjugate-linear dual. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, let $u_{\gamma,f}$ be the unique element of the coset $f$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla z}\,dx=0\qquad(z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)).$$
Define the weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ by
$$\bigl(\Lambda_\gamma f\bigr)(g):=\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla V_g}\,dx,$$
where $V_g$ is any representative of $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. The trace quotient identification makes $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ the $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data space with its trace quotient norm. Constants lie in the kernel of $\Lambda_\gamma$, and its range functionals annihilate constants; hence $\Lambda_\gamma$ induces $\dot\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1\to(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*$, the quotient Dirichlet-to-Neumann map used for Calderón stability. Well-posedness, independence from the representative $V_g$, boundedness and the induced quotient map are established by the well-posedness result cited below.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d=2$ with the conductivity class $X_2(R)$ of the Calderón admissible class. For $\gamma\in X_2(R)$ let $\widetilde{\gamma-1}$ be the zero extension of $\gamma-1$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^2$ and set $\gamma_e:=1+\widetilde{\gamma-1}$. Define $B:=\max\{1,M,m^{-1}\}$. There is a constant $C_1$ depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R$ such that
$$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_1|h|\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^2).$$
For every finite $p>2B$ there is $C_p<\infty$, depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R,p$, such that
$$\sup_{\gamma\in X_2(R)}\ \sup_{|h|\le t}\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_p t^{1/p}\qquad(t\ge0).$$
The outer supremum is taken in $[0,\infty]$, with $\sup\varnothing=0$. The extension is an almost-everywhere measurable class; no pointwise continuity is asserted.

before.statement:
Let $M\subset\mathbb R^{d_a}$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n\ge d$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a bounded domain, and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and nonpolynomial. Fix finite input and output channel dimensions. A generalized Fourier neural operator is a map $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^{d_{in}})\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_{out}})$ of the form
$$\Psi=Q\circ R\circ F\circ L_L\circ\cdots\circ L_1\circ E\circ S.$$
Here $S$ is a pointwise finite-dimensional affine network, $S(h)(x)=s(x,h(x))$; $E$ is a continuous linear chart-lifting map from manifold functions to multichannel functions on $\mathbb T^n$; each $L_\ell$ acts on periodic channel fields by a fixed matrix channel map plus a continuous periodic channel bias $b_\ell(x)$ and a finite Fourier-multiplier convolution, followed coordinatewise by $\sigma$; $F:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{c})\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^{r})$ is a continuous linear dimension-reduction layer
$$ (Fv)(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\int_{\mathbb T^{n-d}}K(z)v(x_1,\ldots,x_d,z)\,dz,$$

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ be a real conductivity. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, let $dS$ be surface measure, and set
$$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

Regard $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ as a real Hilbert space with its complex $L^2$ norm. The exact-data inverse map
$$\Psi^\star:\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)=\gamma,$$
is well-defined and satisfies

Fix $d\ge2$, a bounded connected smooth domain $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, a fixed collar $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, an admissible conductivity class $X_d(R)$ with fixed ellipticity and regularity parameters, a compact perturbation set $K\subset L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$, and a threshold $\delta\ge0$. Let $K_\delta=\{\eta\in K:\|\eta\|_2\le\delta\}$ and
$$\mathcal Z=\{(\kappa_\gamma+\eta,\gamma):\gamma\in X_d(R),\ \eta\in K_\delta\}$$
in $\mathcal H\times\mathcal Y$, where $\mathcal H=L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ is viewed as a real Hilbert space, $\mathcal Y=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $\mathfrak R f=(\operatorname{Re}f,\operatorname{Im}f)\in L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ is the isometric realification. Assume $\mathcal Z$ is nonempty and compact, and set $X=\{x\in\mathcal H:(x,y)\in\mathcal Z\text{ for some }y\in\mathcal Y\}$. Fix a smooth globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation $\sigma_0$.

Choose once and for all a finite smooth boundary chart family and square partition of unity as in the boundary chart-lifting lemma. For every positive finite channel count $c$, let $G_c$ be the componentwise application of this same scalar chart construction, so $G_c:L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb R^c)\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{J^2c})$ for its fixed number $J^2$ of chart pairs. Each pointwise lift $S_0$ receives the two realified input channels; if its output has $c$ channels, take $E=G_c$. The family $(G_c)$, the chart weights and the output restriction $R$ to $\Omega$ are fixed and have no trainable parameters; $c$ is already part of the counted finite architecture index, not an additional scalar parameter. Write $n=2d-2$. The dimension-reduction layer $F$ has a matrix-valued kernel on $\mathbb T^{n-d}$; if $n=d$, take $F$ to be the identity. For each integer $s\ge1$ and $B>0$, define $\mathcal F_{s,B}\subset C(X,\mathcal Y)$ as the restrictions to $X$ of maps $x\mapsto\Phi(\mathfrak R x)$, where $\Phi$ is a generalized Fourier neural operator with the following finite parameterization:

1. The pointwise lift $S_0$ and output network $Q$ are fully connected finite-dimensional networks. At each point they receive the fixed ambient coordinate and the current real field vector; hidden affine layers are followed coordinatewise by $\sigma_0$, and the final layer is affine. Their depths, hidden widths and all variable output channel widths are at most $s$; the final output of $Q$ is the single real target channel.
2. The Fourier-operator stack has at most $s$ layers and at most $s$ channels in each layer. Each channel matrix is a trainable real matrix. Each Fourier multiplier has matrix coefficients $R_{\ell,k}$ supported on $\|k\|_\infty\le s$, with $R_{\ell,-k}=\overline{R_{\ell,k}}$ so real fields remain real. Each coordinate bias $b_\ell$ is a real trigonometric polynomial on $\mathbb T^n$ supported on the same finite mode range.
3. The dimension-reduction kernel is a real matrix-valued trigonometric polynomial
$$K(z)=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty\le s}K_ke^{2\pi i k\cdot z},\qquad K_{-k}=\overline{K_k},$$
with coefficients of the dimensions required by the adjacent channel counts.
4. The number of independent trainable real scalar coefficients in all pointwise networks, channel matrices, Fourier multipliers, coordinate biases, and dimension-reduction kernels together is at most $s$. For complex Fourier coefficients, independent real and imaginary parts are counted separately, subject to conjugate symmetry. Every trainable real scalar coefficient has absolute value at most $B$. The fixed activation, chart maps, partition weights, realification, restriction, and Fourier basis are not trainable parameters.

For each fixed $s$, only finitely many architecture index tuples occur; equip their disjoint union of bounded real parameter boxes with its Borel structure, and give $\mathcal F_{s,B}$ the Borel sigma-algebra induced by the supremum norm on $C(X,\mathcal Y)$. Consider only $s,B$ for which this class is nonempty and $\sup_{\Psi\in\mathcal F_{s,B},\,x\in X}\|\Psi(x)\|_{\mathcal Y}<\infty$. For $z=(x,y)\in\mathcal Z$ and $\Psi\in\mathcal F_{s,B}$, define $\ell(z,\Psi)=\|\Psi(x)-y\|_{\mathcal Y}^2$. For a Borel probability law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, put $R_P(\Psi)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}\ell(Z,\Psi)$ and $\widehat R_N(\Psi)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(Z_i,\Psi)$ for iid $Z_i\sim P$. Determine the minimax excess-risk behavior
$$\mathfrak R_N(s,B):=\inf_{\widehat\Psi_N}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Z)}\mathbb E_{P^N}\left[R_P(\widehat\Psi_N)-\inf_{\Psi\in\mathcal F_{s,B}}R_P(\Psi)\right],$$
where $\mathcal P(\mathcal Z)$ is the set of Borel probability laws on $\mathcal Z$ and the infimum is over Borel learners $\widehat\Psi_N:\mathcal Z^N\to\mathcal F_{s,B}$. Characterize growth regimes $s=s_N$, $B=B_N$ in which estimation and continuum approximation errors can be balanced while retaining the deterministic noise term $C_\star\omega_\star(\delta)$.

Let $K_\delta=\{\eta\in K:\|\eta\|_2\le\delta\}$ and
$$\mathcal Z=\{(\kappa_\gamma+\eta,\gamma):\gamma\in X_d(R),\ \eta\in K_\delta\}$$
in $\mathcal H\times\mathcal Y$, where $\mathcal H=L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ is viewed as a real Hilbert space, $\mathcal Y=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $\mathfrak R f=(\operatorname{Re}f,\operatorname{Im}f)\in L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ is the isometric realification. $$\|\widetilde\Psi^\star(f)-\widetilde\Psi^\star(g)\|_{\mathcal Y}\le C_\star\omega_\star(\|f-g\|_{\mathcal H})\qquad(f,g\in\mathcal H).$$

The family $(G_c)$, the chart weights and the output restriction $R$ to $\Omega$ are fixed and have no trainable parameters; $c$ is already part of the counted finite architecture index, not an additional scalar parameter. 1. The pointwise lift $S_0$ and output network $Q$ are fully connected finite-dimensional networks. At each point they receive the fixed ambient coordinate and the current real field vector; hidden affine layers are followed coordinatewise by $\sigma_0$, and the final layer is affine. Their depths, hidden widths and all variable output channel widths are at most $s$; the final output of $Q$ is the single real target channel.

Each Fourier multiplier has matrix coefficients $R_{\ell,k}$ supported on $\|k\|_\infty\le s$, with $R_{\ell,-k}=\overline{R_{\ell,k}}$ so real fields remain real. Each coordinate bias $b_\ell$ is a real trigonometric polynomial on $\mathbb T^n$ supported on the same finite mode range.
3. The dimension-reduction kernel is a real matrix-valued trigonometric polynomial
$$K(z)=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty\le s}K_ke^{2\pi i k\cdot z},\qquad K_{-k}=\overline{K_k},$$
with coefficients of the dimensions required by the adjacent channel counts.
4. The number of independent trainable real scalar coefficients in all pointwise networks, channel matrices, Fourier multipliers, coordinate biases, and dimension-reduction kernels together is at most $s$. For complex Fourier coefficients, independent real and imaginary parts are counted separately, subject to conjugate symmetry. Every trainable real scalar coefficient has absolute value at most $B$. For each fixed $s$, only finitely many architecture index tuples occur; equip their disjoint union of bounded real parameter boxes with its Borel structure, and give $\mathcal F_{s,B}$ the Borel sigma-algebra induced by the supremum norm on $C(X,\mathcal Y)$. For a Borel probability law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, put $R_P(\Psi)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}\ell(Z,\Psi)$ and $\widehat R_N(\Psi)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(Z_i,\Psi)$ for iid $Z_i\sim P$. Determine the minimax excess-risk behavior
$$\mathfrak R_N(s,B):=\inf_{\widehat\Psi_N}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Z)}\mathbb E_{P^N}\left[R_P(\widehat\Psi_N)-\inf_{\Psi\in\mathcal F_{s,B}}R_P(\Psi)\right],$$
where $\mathcal P(\mathcal Z)$ is the set of Borel probability laws on $\mathcal Z$ and the infimum is over Borel learners $\widehat\Psi_N:\mathcal Z^N\to\mathcal F_{s,B}$. before.statement: Let $\Omega=B((1/2,1/2),1/4)\subset(0,1)^2$, let $\Omega'=B((1/2,1/2),1/8)$, and fix $m=1/2$, $M=3/2$, and contrast $a=1/4$. For every integer $N\ge1$, put $q=\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$, choose $N$ distinct cell centers from the $q\times q$ grid in $[7/16,9/16]^2$, set $r_N=1/(32q)$, and define $\gamma_N=1+a\mathbf1_{E_N}$, where $E_N$ is the union of the radius-$r_N$ disks about those centers. Then every $\gamma_N$ is a real, uniformly elliptic, individually finite-BV conductivity equal to $1$ outside $\Omega'$, but $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)\ge(\pi a/32)\sqrt N$. Hence the family has no common finite BV bound $R$ and is not contained in any one class $X_2(R)$ as $N$ varies. This is a non-applicability example for a fixed uniform BV theorem, not a counterexample to its conclusion for members of that class.

before.statement: Let $\mathcal H=L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)$ and $\mathcal Y=L^2(\Omega)$ for a bounded smooth EIT domain. Given any nonempty finite sample set $S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\mathcal H$, any $x_*\in\mathcal H\setminus S$, and any $y_*\in\mathcal Y\setminus\{0\}$, there are continuous maps $F_0,F_1:\mathcal H\to\mathcal Y$ that agree at every sample input and differ by $y_*$ at $x_*$. Therefore exact fit on finitely many inputs alone cannot identify an arbitrary continuous inverse map. A continuum FNO approximation theorem concerns the full $L^2$ kernel input and $L^2$ conductivity output on a compact set; a finite-element experiment reports a finite discretization and finite train/test sample. Neither finite-data fit nor a discretized operator matrix supplies the continuum theorem's uniform bound or a statistical generalization guarantee.

before.statement:
Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure and fix the real orthonormal Fourier basis
$$\phi_1(x)=1,\qquad \phi_{2k}(x)=\sqrt2\cos(kx),\qquad \phi_{2k+1}(x)=\sqrt2\sin(kx)\quad(k\ge1).$$
Use this basis to identify the real Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R)$. Fix integers $N,m\ge1$ and parameters $s,p,R,\sigma>0$, and define
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad (A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j,\qquad \mathcal X_p(R)=A_p\Theta_s(R).$$
The inverse map $G^\dagger:\mathcal X_p(R)\to\ell^2$ is $G^\dagger(A_p\theta)=\theta$. For $m\ge1$, let $P_m$ retain the first $m$ Fourier coefficients and let $I_m:\mathbb R^m\to\ell^2$ append zero coordinates.

Fix a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial function $\sigma_0:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, called the activation. For $x\in\mathbb R^m$, form the scalar input field $\bar u_0(x;z)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\phi_j(z)$. A pointwise affine lift $u_0(x;z)=V_{\mathrm{in}}\bar u_0(x;z)+b_{\mathrm{in}}$, with $V_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$ and $b_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$, creates $c_0$ channels. For fields $u_\ell(z)\in\mathbb R^{c_\ell}$ with positive integer channel counts $c_\ell$, apply an integer number $D\ge1$ of layers indexed by $\ell=0,\ldots,D-1$:
$$u_{\ell+1}(z)=\sigma_0\!\left(W_\ell u_\ell(z)+b_\ell+(\mathcal K_\ell u_\ell)(z)\right).$$
Here $\sigma_0$ acts coordinatewise, $W_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ and $b_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}}$ are pointwise channel weights, and $\mathcal K_\ell$ is a Fourier multiplier meaning $\widehat{(\mathcal K_\ell u)}(k)=R_{\ell,k}\widehat u(k)$, where $\widehat u(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}u(z)e^{-ikz}\,dz$ is computed componentwise, with matrices $R_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb C^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ satisfying $R_{\ell,-k}=\overline{R_{\ell,k}}$ and $R_{\ell,k}=0$ for $|k|>q$ for some integer cutoff $q\ge0$. A pointwise affine output map $v(x;z)=a_{\mathrm{out}}^\top u_D(z)+b_{\mathrm{out}}$ gives a real scalar field, and the network output is $\Psi_m(x)=(\langle v(x;\cdot),\phi_j\rangle_{L^2})_{j=1}^m$. Let $\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$ be the union of these maps over architectures whose depth, channel counts, Fourier cutoff, and number of real scalar parameters are each at most the integer $S\ge1$, with every trainable parameter bounded in absolute value by $B>0$. A parameter array used at mesh size $m$ is the same array at every other mesh size. For fixed $S$, there are finitely many allowed architecture indices; equip their disjoint union of bounded real parameter boxes with its Borel structure.

Write $\mathcal P(K)$ for the Borel probability laws on a Borel set $K$. For a Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\Theta_s(R)$, draw independent training truths $\theta_i\sim\mu$ and observations
$$X_{i,m}=P_mA_p\theta_i+\eta_{i,m},\qquad Y_{i,m}=P_m\theta_i,\qquad \eta_{i,m}\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m),\quad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with all noises independent, and write $D_{N,m}=((X_{i,m},Y_{i,m}))_{i=1}^N$. A selector is Borel into the finite disjoint union of architecture indices and their bounded parameter boxes, and its realized map minimizes the empirical loss. For each $N,m,S,B$, assume there is at least one such selector $\tau$ that, from $D_{N,m}$, returns a minimizer of
$$\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|\Psi(X_{i,m})-Y_{i,m}\|_2^2$$
over $\Psi\in\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$; let $\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)$ be the set of all such selectors. At test time, draw an independent $\theta\sim\mu$ and $\eta_m\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m)$, and define
$$\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)=\inf_{\tau\in\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)}\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\Theta_s(R))}E\left\|I_m\tau(D_{N,m})(P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m)-\theta\right\|_{\ell^2}^2.$$
Also define $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$ by the same infimum over all Borel predictors from $(D_{N,m},X_m)$ to $\mathbb R^m$, with $X_m=P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m$. Determine matching minimax upper and lower rates for $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)$ jointly in $N,m,S,B,p,s,R,\sigma$. In particular, characterize the joint growth regimes of $m=m_N$ and $S=S_N$ that separate statistical estimation, neural-operator approximation, and continuum truncation error, and determine when the bounded shared-parameter Fourier architecture attains the unrestricted rate $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$.

after.title: Joint sample and mesh rates for neural inverse maps
after.statement:
Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure and fix the real orthonormal Fourier basis
$$\phi_1(x)=1,\qquad \phi_{2k}(x)=\sqrt2\cos(kx),\qquad \phi_{2k+1}(x)=\sqrt2\sin(kx)\quad(k\ge1).$$
Use this basis to identify the real Hilbert space $\ell^2=\ell^2(\mathbb N_{>0};\mathbb R)$, where $\mathbb N_{>0}=\{1,2,\ldots\}$, with $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R)$. Fix integers $N,m\ge1$ and parameters $s,p,R,\sigma>0$, and define
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad (A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j,\qquad \mathcal X_p(R)=A_p\Theta_s(R).$$
The inverse map $G^\dagger:\mathcal X_p(R)\to\ell^2$ is $G^\dagger(A_p\theta)=\theta$. For $m\ge1$, let $P_m$ retain the first $m$ Fourier coefficients and let $I_m:\mathbb R^m\to\ell^2$ append zero coordinates.

Fix a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial function $\sigma_0:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, called the activation. For $x\in\mathbb R^m$, form the scalar input field $\bar u_0(x;z)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\phi_j(z)$. A pointwise affine lift $u_0(x;z)=V_{\mathrm{in}}\bar u_0(x;z)+b_{\mathrm{in}}$, with $V_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$ and $b_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$, creates $c_0$ channels. For fields $u_\ell(z)\in\mathbb R^{c_\ell}$ with positive integer channel counts $c_\ell$, apply an integer number $D\ge1$ of layers indexed by $\ell=0,\ldots,D-1$:
$$u_{\ell+1}(z)=\sigma_0\!\left(W_\ell u_\ell(z)+b_\ell+(\mathcal K_\ell u_\ell)(z)\right).$$
Here $\sigma_0$ acts coordinatewise, $W_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ and $b_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}}$ are pointwise channel weights, and $\mathcal K_\ell$ is a Fourier multiplier meaning $\widehat{(\mathcal K_\ell u)}(k)=R_{\ell,k}\widehat u(k)$, where $\widehat u(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}u(z)e^{-ikz}\,dz$ is computed componentwise, with matrices $R_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb C^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ satisfying $R_{\ell,-k}=\overline{R_{\ell,k}}$ and $R_{\ell,k}=0$ for $|k|>q$ for some integer cutoff $q\ge0$. A pointwise affine output map $v(x;z)=a_{\mathrm{out}}^\top u_D(z)+b_{\mathrm{out}}$ gives a real scalar field, and the network output is $\Psi_m(x)=(\langle v(x;\cdot),\phi_j\rangle_{L^2})_{j=1}^m$. Let $\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$ be the union of these maps over architectures whose depth, channel counts, Fourier cutoff, and number of real scalar parameters are each at most the integer $S\ge1$, with every trainable parameter bounded in absolute value by $B>0$. A parameter array used at mesh size $m$ is the same array at every other mesh size. For fixed $S$, there are finitely many allowed architecture indices; equip their disjoint union of bounded real parameter boxes with its Borel structure.

Write $\mathcal P(K)$ for the Borel probability laws on a Borel set $K$. For a Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\Theta_s(R)$, draw independent training truths $\theta_i\sim\mu$ and observations
$$X_{i,m}=P_mA_p\theta_i+\eta_{i,m},\qquad Y_{i,m}=P_m\theta_i,\qquad \eta_{i,m}\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m),\quad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with all noises independent, and write $D_{N,m}=((X_{i,m},Y_{i,m}))_{i=1}^N$. A selector is Borel into the finite disjoint union of architecture indices and their bounded parameter boxes, and its realized map minimizes the empirical loss. For each $N,m,S,B$ with $\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}\ne\varnothing$, assume there is at least one such selector $\tau$ that, from $D_{N,m}$, returns a minimizer of
$$\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|\Psi(X_{i,m})-Y_{i,m}\|_2^2$$
over $\Psi\in\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$; let $\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)$ be the set of all such selectors, and set it to $\varnothing$ when $\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}=\varnothing$. At test time, draw an independent $\theta\sim\mu$ and $\eta_m\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m)$, and define
$$\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)=\inf_{\tau\in\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)}\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\Theta_s(R))}E\left\|I_m\tau(D_{N,m})(P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m)-\theta\right\|_{\ell^2}^2.$$
Use the convention $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so an empty architecture class has infinite ERM risk. Also define $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$ by the same infimum over all Borel predictors from $(D_{N,m},X_m)$ to $\mathbb R^m$, with $X_m=P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m$. Determine matching minimax upper and lower rates for $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)$ jointly in $N,m,S,B,p,s,R,\sigma$. In particular, characterize the joint growth regimes of $m=m_N$ and $S=S_N$ that separate statistical estimation, neural-operator approximation, and continuum truncation error, and determine when the bounded shared-parameter Fourier architecture attains the unrestricted rate $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$.

before.title: A diagonal inverse has an explicit Fourier truncation error
before.statement:
Let $p,s,R>0$, $m\ge1$, $\theta\in\ell^2$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2$, and let $(A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j$. Given data $y=A_p\theta+\eta$ with $\|\eta\|_{\ell^2}\le\delta$, the mesh-$m$ truncated inverse is $g_m(y)=(j^py_j)_{j\le m}$ with zero output coordinates for $j>m$. It satisfies the continuum error bound
$$\|g_m(y)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}\le m^p\delta+R(m+1)^{-s}.$$
This separates measurement-noise amplification from the mesh truncation tail; it makes no statistical or neural-operator claim.
before.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the truncation and norm estimates are explicit.

after.title: A diagonal inverse has an explicit Fourier truncation error
after.statement:

It satisfies the continuum error bound

before.title: Finite samples cannot identify every Lipschitz inverse map uniformly
before.statement:
Let $N\ge1$ and let $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in[0,1]$ be arbitrary training inputs. For every deterministic learning rule that returns a prediction function $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ from the observed pairs $(x_i,f(x_i))$, there are two $1$-Lipschitz functions $f_0,f_1:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ agreeing with each other and taking the common value $0$ at every training input but satisfying
$$\|f_1-f_0\|_{\infty}\ge\frac{1}{2(N+1)}.$$
Consequently, at the midpoint of a largest sample-free interval, the returned prediction function $g$ has absolute prediction error at least $1/(4(N+1))$ for at least one of these two indistinguishable target functions.
before.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the construction uses finitely many sample points.

before.statement:
Consider the complete original Fourier architecture and diagonal inverse question reproduced below. For every odd integer $m\ge3$, every $N\ge1$, and every admissible bounded parameter class with a measurable empirical minimizer, its risk satisfies
$$\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)\ge\frac{R^2(3^p-2^p)^2}{4\,3^{2(p+s)}}>0.$$
The same bound holds for every measurable learner whose realized predictor belongs to the stated coordinate-free Fourier class, whether or not it minimizes empirical risk. On the other hand, the unrestricted risk tends to zero as $m\to\infty$ for fixed $p,s,R,\sigma>0$, independently of $N$. Thus no growth of $N,S,B$ can make this original architecture attain the vanishing unrestricted risk along an odd-mesh subsequence. This is a partial resolution: no complete joint bounded-class rate, or corresponding fixed positive even-mesh floor, is asserted. The original question is retained verbatim under Original question.

before.statement: In $\mathbb R^2$ take $\Phi=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ with $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(0,1)$, and $a_3=(1,1)$. Its intensity map on classes modulo $x\sim -x$ is $[x]\mapsto(x_1^2,x_2^2,(x_1+x_2)^2)$. Every pair is linearly independent, so every pair spans $\mathbb R^2$; consequently, for every partition one side spans $\mathbb R^2$. Equality of the displayed triples therefore forces two signals to be equal up to a global sign.

before.title: Repeated measurements with correlated noise
before.statement: Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N(0,1)$ and take two repeated observations with $A=(1,1)^T$ and noise covariance $\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $-1<\rho<1$. The matrix $\Gamma_\rho$ is positive definite. The expected information gain is $\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}\right)$. In particular, correlation $\rho=\frac12$ gives $\frac12\log(7/3)$, less than the independent-noise value $\frac12\log 3$ at $\rho=0$.

before.title: Information gain on a singular prior support
before.statement: Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, so its support is the first coordinate axis. With unit-variance Gaussian noise, compare the one-coordinate measurements $A_\perp=(0,1)$ and $A_\parallel=(1,0)$. Their expected information gains are $0$ and $\frac12\log 2$, respectively. The log-determinant formula remains defined although $C$ is singular.

before.title: Discrete linear input-state-output experiments
before.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers, and let $h>0$ be a fixed
sampling interval. A real **discrete linear input-state-output experiment** of
state dimension $d$, input dimension $m$, output dimension $p$, and horizon
$q$ consists of matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$, an
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and known inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$ in $\mathbb R^m$. The states are defined by
$$x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\qquad(0\le k<q-1),$$
and the exact sampled outputs at times $kh$ are $y_k=Cx_k$ for
$0\le k<q$. When observations are perturbed, the observed outputs are
$\widetilde y_k=y_k+\eta_k$ for deterministic error vectors
$\eta_k\in\mathbb R^p$; the exact-data convention is $\eta_k=0$ for all $k$.
No probability law is assigned to the errors. A numerical or discretization
error that changes the forward map is distinct from this additive observation
error.

For an impulse-response experiment with zero initial state, first input
$u_0=v\in\mathbb R^m$, and later inputs zero, the **Markov parameters** are
$$M_k:=CA^kB\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R)\qquad(k\ge0),$$
so the output one sample after the impulse is $y_{k+1}=M_kv$. Matrix powers
use $A^0=I_d$ and $A^{k+1}=A^kA$. If $d=0$, the state space consists of its
single zero vector and the matrices have the corresponding empty shapes.
before.strategy: Specify the state, input, output, time-indexing, noise, and impulse-response conventions directly in finite-dimensional coordinates.

after.title: Discrete linear input-state-output experiments
after.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers, and let $h>0$ be a fixed
sampling interval. A real **discrete linear input-state-output experiment** of
state dimension $d$, input dimension $m$, output dimension $p$, and horizon
$q$ consists of matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$, an
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and known inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$ in $\mathbb R^m$. The states are defined by
$$x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\qquad(0\le k<q-1),$$
and the exact sampled outputs at times $kh$ are $y_k=Cx_k$ for
$0\le k<q$. When observations are perturbed, the observed outputs are
$\widetilde y_k=y_k+\eta_k$ for deterministic error vectors
$\eta_k\in\mathbb R^p$; the exact-data convention is $\eta_k=0$ for all $k$.
No probability law is assigned to the errors. A numerical or discretization
error that changes the forward map is distinct from this additive observation
error.

For the fixed matrices $A,B,C$, the **Markov parameters** are
$$M_k:=CA^kB\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R)\qquad(k\ge0),$$
interpreted using the infinite-horizon impulse experiment: extend the same
state and output equations to all $k\ge0$, with zero initial state,
$u_0=v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $u_k=0$ for $k\ge1$. Its output at sample $k+1$
is $y_{k+1}=M_kv$ for every $k\ge0$. The horizon-$q$ restriction records this
identity only for $0\le k<q-1$; when $q=1$, it records only $y_0=0$ and has
no input samples. Matrix powers
use $A^0=I_d$ and $A^{k+1}=A^kA$. If $d=0$, the state space consists of its
single zero vector and the matrices have the corresponding empty shapes.
after.strategy: Specify the state, input, output, time-indexing, noise, and impulse-response conventions directly in finite-dimensional coordinates.

before.title: Wirtinger presentation from a finite diagram code

references.title: Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §§2–3
Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36

before.statement:
The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

After validation, traverse the oriented knot once from $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. In the verified counterclockwise cyclic order, the under-half-edge immediately following it is the target side $a_t$; the other under-half-edge is the source side $a_s$. Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. The orientation of each positive meridian is fixed by requiring the oriented knot tangent followed by its normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

before.title: Framed knots, self-linking, and the Seifert framing
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot
$K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, its normal bundle is
$\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, oriented so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a
positive basis of a normal fibre gives the ambient orientation. A **framing**
of $K$ is a homotopy class through smooth nowhere-zero sections of $\nu K$.
The normal bundle is made a smooth vector bundle under this axiom; a framed
knot includes the section class as data, not a choice made afterwards. For the
relative integer use the round metric transferred from the unit sphere in
$\mathbb R^4$ by the explicit diffeomorphism
$$x\longmapsto\left(\frac{2x}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2},\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2-1}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2}\right),\qquad\infty\longmapsto(0,0,0,1).$$
It induces a smooth bundle metric on $\nu K$. The resulting winding number is
independent of the metric: any two smooth fibre metrics interpolate through
positive metrics and the corresponding angle maps are homotopic.

Given a reference framing $[s_0]$ and another framing $[s_1]$, use a bundle
metric and the positive quarter-turn $J$ on each oriented normal plane. Choose
representatives $s_0,s_1$ and normalize both to unit sections
$\widehat s_i(x):=s_i(x)/\lVert s_i(x)\rVert$. Write
$$\widehat s_1(x)=\cos\theta(x)\widehat s_0(x)+\sin\theta(x)J\widehat s_0(x).$$
The resulting map $S^1\to S^1$ has a continuous angle lift along a parameter
interval $[0,1]$: subdivide into finitely many intervals whose images lie in
open semicircles and choose consecutive local arguments agreeing at endpoints.
Since the map is closed, the lift satisfies $\theta(1)-\theta(0)=2\pi m$ for
some $m\in\mathbb Z$; different lifts differ by a constant multiple of
$2\pi$, and homotopies keep $m$ fixed. Conversely, the difference between
$\theta(t)$ and $\theta(0)+2\pi mt$ is periodic, so linear interpolation of
these angles gives a homotopy to the degree-$m$ rotation of $\widehat s_0$.
Every integer occurs by such a rotation. Thus $m$ classifies the framing class
relative to $[s_0]$ and gives the **relative framing integer**. Once a reference
framing is supplied, the framing classes are an integer torsor; no absolute
integer is assigned before choosing a reference.

The **self-linking number** of a framed knot $(K,[s])$ is the linking number
of $K$ with a sufficiently small push-off along $s$, oriented parallel to $K$.
The push-off and its integer are independent of the representative section,
small radius, and normalized tubular chart by the preceding well-definedness
result.

If a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ is supplied with boundary $K$, its
**Seifert framing relative to $\Sigma$** is the homotopy class of the inward
unit conormal to $K$ in $\Sigma$, viewed as a nonzero normal section to $K$ in
$S^3$. This definition is relative to the supplied surface; it neither asserts
that every knot bounds such a surface nor asserts the self-linking-zero result.

before.statement:
Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

before.statement: Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For an oriented Seifert surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary $K$ and ordered basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, let $V$ be the Seifert matrix with entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Here $\operatorname{lk}$ is the integer linking number of disjoint oriented cycles in $S^3$, and $a_i^+$ is a small push-off in the positive normal direction, chosen so that the positive normal followed by the oriented basis of $F$ gives the orientation of $S^3$. Use the standard knot-invariant conventions $\Delta_K(t)=\det(V-tV^T)$ up to units $\pm t^k$ and $\sigma_{-1}(K)=\operatorname{sign}(2(V+V^T))$, where the matrix sign is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues; independence of the chosen surface and basis is part of the Seifert-form invariance theorems. Let $T$ be the standard right-handed trefoil, let $T^*$ be its image under a fixed orientation-reversing reflection of $S^3$, and let $-T^*$ be that image with reversed knot orientation. Define $G=T\#T$ and $Q=T\#(-T^*)$. Then $\Delta_G(t)\doteq\Delta_Q(t)\doteq(t^2-t+1)^2$, and $|\sigma_{-1}(G)|=4$ while $\sigma_{-1}(Q)=0$. The oriented prime-factor multisets of $G$ and $Q$ are different. Thus equality of Alexander polynomials does not determine the prime knot summands.

before.statement:
Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots, and let $K\#J$ be their oriented connected sum for a connected-sum datum using the fixed gluing convention. Then

$$\Delta_{K\#J}(t)\doteq \Delta_K(t)\Delta_J(t),$$

where each $\Delta$ is the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the one-variable Alexander module and $\doteq$ means equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. The statement is independent of the local connected-sum choices and of the Seifert surfaces and bases used to compute the polynomials.

references.title: John Milnor, Link Groups
Ryan Stees, Milnor’s Invariants for Knots and Links in Closed Orientable 3-Manifolds
references.locator: §2.5, printed pp. 16–18 (PDF pp. 24–26)

before.statement:
Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars. For closure, fix once and for all a standard zero-framed unknotted embedding $\Psi:D^2\times(\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z)\hookrightarrow S^3$, and identify $C$ with $\Psi(D^2\times[0,1])$. Adjoin to each strand the fixed product arc $\Psi(\{p_i\}\times[1,2])$, oriented from its top endpoint to its bottom endpoint. These disjoint outside arcs, with the fixed endpoint collars, define the closure and retain the component labels; arbitrary knotted or braided replacement arcs are not allowed.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

before.title: The maximal abelian cover retracts to a compact link exterior

references.title: Allen Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §1.3, homotopy lifting and covering classification

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. $$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$

before.title: String-link exterior homology and end-meridian maps

references.title: John Milnor, Link Groups
references.locator: §2 and Lemma 2, PDF pp. 2–3

references.title: Ryan Stees, Milnor’s Invariants for Knots and Links in Closed Orientable 3-Manifolds

before.statement:
Use integral homology. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented smooth link in $S^3$ with chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes and exterior $E_L$. Then $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive meridians as its ordered basis. Each boundary torus $T_i$ has a product basis consisting of its positive meridian and a degree-one section. There is a unique degree-one class on $T_i$ whose image has zero $i$th meridian coordinate; this class is primitive and has a simple closed representative.

Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component string link with chosen disjoint product tubes in $D^2\times[0,1]$, exterior $X_\tau$, and bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$. Then each $\pi_1(P_\pm)$ is free of rank $r$. Positive endpoint meridians with the compatible accesses transported from a point-punctured-disk spine form an ordered free basis. For arbitrary independently chosen access paths, the corresponding meridian is $c_i m_i c_i^{-1}$, where $m_i$ is the compatible-stem meridian and $c_i$ is the recorded access-path difference; these conjugates need not be a free basis. In particular $H_1(P_\pm;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, and $H_2(P_\pm;\mathbb Z)=0$. The exterior satisfies $H_1(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$ and $H_2(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)=0$. Each end inclusion sends its ordered positive meridian basis to the ordered positive meridian basis of $H_1(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)$. Consequently both induced homomorphisms on $H_1$ are isomorphisms and both induced homomorphisms on $H_2$ are surjective.

before.title: Surgery presentation from a Seifert surface
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ bound a connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$. Choose a disk-band decomposition of $F$ with one disk and $2g$ bands, and use its band-core basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ to form the positive-push Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. For $q\ge2$, define the symmetric block matrix $M_q(V)$ of size $2g(q-1)$ by specifying its $2g\times2g$ blocks, indexed by $1\le k,\ell\le q-1$:
$$(M_q(V))_{k\ell}=\begin{cases}V+V^T,&k=\ell,\\-V^T,&\ell=k+1,\\-V,&k=\ell+1,\\0,&|k-\ell|\ge2.\end{cases}$$
Push the interior of $F$ into $B^4$ while keeping $K$ on $S^3=\partial B^4$, cut $B^4$ along a thickened copy of the pushed-in surface, and take $q$ copies. For $i=1,\ldots,q-1$, glue the positive face of copy $i$ to the negative face of copy $i+1$ by reflecting the normal coordinate; do not glue the last positive face to the first negative face. Call the resulting $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $W_q(F)$. It has one $0$-handle and $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles, and its framed attaching link has linking matrix $M_q(V)$. The boundary branched cover, with the boundary marking induced by the covering map, is $\Sigma_q(K)$.

after.title: Surgery presentation from a Seifert surface
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ bound a connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$. Choose a disk-band decomposition of $F$ with one disk and $2g$ bands, and use its band-core basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ to form the positive-push Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. For $q\ge2$, define the symmetric block matrix $M_q(V)$ of size $2g(q-1)$ by specifying its $2g\times2g$ blocks, indexed by $1\le k,\ell\le q-1$:
$$(M_q(V))_{k\ell}=\begin{cases}V+V^T,&k=\ell,\\-V^T,&\ell=k+1,\\-V,&k=\ell+1,\\0,&|k-\ell|\ge2.\end{cases}$$
Push the interior of $F$ into $B^4$ while keeping $K$ on $S^3=\partial B^4$, and let $W_q(F)$ be the actual $q$-fold cyclic branched cover along that pushed-in surface. Use the following disk-band handle model of this cover. Cut $B^4$ along the three-dimensional track of the push-in isotopy; the cut-open manifold is again a $4$-ball and its boundary contains the thickened surface $\bar F=(F\times[-1,1])/\sim$, where $(x,t)\sim(x,t')$ for $x\in\partial F$. Write $\bar F^\pm=\{(x,t)\in\bar F:\pm t\ge0\}$. Take $q$ copies of this cut-open ball and, for $i=1,\ldots,q-1$, glue $\bar F_i^+$ to $\bar F_{i+1}^-$ by $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$. The Akbulut–Kirby construction identifies this handle model with $W_q(F)$; the last-to-first gluing is unnecessary for the underlying manifold in this model. This is a statement about the isotopy-track handle model, not an assertion that an open chain of normal-disk sectors is already the cyclic covering map. The resulting handle presentation has one $0$-handle and $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles, and its framed attaching link has linking matrix $M_q(V)$. The boundary branched cover, with the boundary marking induced by the covering map of $W_q(F)$, is $\Sigma_q(K)$.

before.title: Levine–Tristram Hermitian form and signature

references.title: Anthony Conway, The Levine–Tristram signature: a survey, 2019–20 MATRIX Annals (2021), pp. 31–56 (arXiv:1903.04477)
references.locator: §2.1, printed pp. 2–4: Hermitian form convention; §2.4, printed p. 6: averaged signature at roots; complete 18-page PDF inspected.

before.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface with oriented boundary $K$, let $V$ be the matrix of the Seifert pairing $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis, and let $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$. Define the **Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix** by
$$H_\omega(V)=(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T.$$
It is Hermitian because $V$ is real and $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, both counted with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted. When $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, define $\sigma_\omega(K)$ to be this signature. At a root $\omega_0\ne1$ of $\Delta_K$, define $\sigma_{\omega_0}(K)$ to be the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided limits of $\sigma_{e^{i\theta}}(K)$ as $\theta$ approaches an argument of $\omega_0$ from below and above. The invariance and one-sided-existence lemmas justify treating these values as independent of the chosen surface and basis.

before.statement:
Assume full AC. For an even-order integral matrix $V$ that is the Seifert matrix of a knot, **S-equivalence** means the equivalence relation generated by integral unimodular congruences $V\mapsto P^TVP$ with $\det P=\pm1$ and the following two enlargements, for column vectors $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $z\in\mathbb Z$:

$$E_0(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_1(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$
and their reverses. For an assignment $P$ of an integer polynomial in $z$ to each ambient-isotopy class of oriented links, call $P$ **Conway-normalized** when $P_U(z)=1$ for the unknot $U$ and
$$P_{L_+}(z)-P_{L_-}(z)=z\,P_{L_0}(z)$$
whenever the three oriented links agree outside one crossing ball and inside it are respectively the positive crossing, negative crossing, and orientation-compatible smoothing; positive means $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})>0$, where $v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under}$ are the projected oriented tangent vectors and $P$ is oriented so the viewing normal followed by a positive basis of $P$ is ambient-positive. The smoothing reconnects the four oriented half-arcs in the unique noncrossing way compatible with their directions. No existence of such an assignment is presupposed: the Seifert-determinant lemma constructs a unique assignment and denotes it by $\nabla_L(z)$. For a knot, let $\Delta_K^\#(t)$ be the unique associate of its Alexander polynomial satisfying $\Delta_K^\#(1)=1$ and $\Delta_K^\#(t^{-1})=\Delta_K^\#(t)$; existence and uniqueness follow from the Alexander-normalization corollary. Set $z=t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2}$, with $t^{1/2}$ a formal Laurent variable, and use $\Delta_K^\#(t)=\nabla_K(z)$ as the normalization convention.

before.title: A Dehn twist of Heegaard gluing is integral surgery

references.title: Nikolai Saveliev, Lectures on the Topology of 3-Manifolds
references.locator: Lemma 2.2 and proof, Lecture 2 §2.2, printed pp. 33–34

before.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M=H_-\cup_\varphi H_+$ be a Heegaard splitting of a closed oriented smooth $3$-manifold, let $\Sigma=\partial H_-=\partial H_+$, and let $c\subset\Sigma$ be an embedded circle with a chosen annular neighbourhood. If $\varphi$ is replaced by $\varphi\circ\tau_c$ or $\varphi\circ\tau_c^{-1}$, where $\tau_c$ is a Dehn twist in the chosen annular coordinates, the resulting oriented $3$-manifold is obtained from $M$ by one surgery on a knot $K$ obtained by pushing $c$ into the interior of $H_-$. The annulus between $c$ and the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood of $K$ supplies a framing; the surgery meridian is identified with $\mu+ \lambda_A$ or $\mu-\lambda_A$, according to the twist direction, where $\mu$ is the meridian of $K$ and $\lambda_A$ is the parallel determined by that annulus. Thus the surgery coefficient relative to this framing is integral with absolute value $1$.

before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the standard oriented three-sphere with $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and choose $0<r<1$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

before.statement: Assume full AC. Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be a solid torus. Every connected, two-sided, properly embedded incompressible and boundary-incompressible surface $F\subset V$ with nonempty boundary is a disk, either a meridian disk or a boundary-parallel disk. In particular, if $F$ is not boundary-parallel, it is a meridian disk. Any two smooth meridian disks with the same boundary admit a smooth isotopy of embeddings relative to that boundary, with a boundary-fixing topological ambient extension. If both disks are neat, this can be a smooth ambient isotopy relative to the boundary. In addition, every two-sided embedded torus $T\subset\operatorname{int}V$ has a compressing disk in $V$.
before.axiom_use: The original full AC hypothesis is retained and implies countable choice for the smooth general-position and Schoenflies suppliers. The smooth Loop criterion and new finite relative isotopy suppliers are choice-free. Full AC is also the explicit premise of the TOP cut-piece finite triangulation used in F10.

before.title: Ideal tetrahedron shape and cusp holonomy
before.statement:
Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are

Assign $z$ to the edges $0\infty$ and $1z$, $z'$ to $1\infty$ and $0z$, and $z''$ to $z\infty$ and $01$. For a chosen normal path $\gamma$, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters it cuts off, using the parameter when the corner is on its left and its reciprocal when the corner is on its right.

before.title: Pared hyperbolic structures and volume
before.statement:
A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$

A **hyperbolic structure on the pared pair** $(M,P)$ is such a metric compatible with the pared marking: on the peripheral subgroup of each component of $P$, $\rho$ is injective and its image is conjugate to a discrete group of Euclidean translations fixing $\infty$, of rank one for an annulus and rank two for a torus. These images preserve horoballs based at their fixed ideal point. This compatibility does not assert that an arbitrary incomplete hyperbolic metric has cusp neighborhoods. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **torus cusp** corresponding to a torus component of $P$ is an embedded end neighborhood isometric to a horoball quotient by that component's holonomy image, with its cross-section parallel to the marked boundary torus. A rank-one horoball quotient is the full cusp model for an annular peripheral subgroup; when a structure has totally geodesic boundary, an annular cusp uses the portion between the incident boundary planes and has annular cross-sections. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

before.statement:
Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.
